category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which specific condition is cited as being caused by mutations in a gene for a muscle protein, which are then transmitted in an X-linked recessive pattern?
options: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Xeroderma pigmentosum
Huntington disease
Cystic fibrosis
Sickle cell anemia
correctOption: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
optionExplanations: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the classic example of an X-linked recessive disorder where mutations in the dystrophin gene lead to progressive muscle weakness.
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disorder where defects in nucleotide excision repair proteins prevent the correction of UV-induced DNA damage.
Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by trinucleotide repeat expansion.
Cystic fibrosis is one of the most common autosomal recessive disorders, primarily affecting chloride transport in epithelial cells.
Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a single nucleotide substitution in the beta-globin gene.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which statement regarding the metabolic regulation of mitochondrial traits is accurate based on the genetic characteristics of the organelle?
options: Mitochondrial ribosomes are identical in size and sedimentation to cytosolic 80S ribosomes.
Mitochondrial proteins are exclusively synthesized within the mitochondria.
The mitochondrial RNA polymerase is a multi-subunit complex identical to RNA Pol II.
Mitochondrial genes are transcribed into polycistronic mRNA.
Mitochondrial DNA is resistant to alkaline hydrolysis unlike RNA.
correctOption: Mitochondrial genes are transcribed into polycistronic mRNA.
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial ribosomes are 55S in size, which is smaller than the 80S cytosolic ribosomes.
Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA, synthesized in the cytosol, and then imported into the mitochondria.
Mitochondria contain a single RNA polymerase that more closely resembles bacterial enzymes than the nuclear RNA Polymerase II.
Mitochondria utilize polycistronic mRNA, where one transcript contains information for multiple genes, reflecting their evolutionary origin.
While DNA is resistant to alkaline hydrolysis (unlike RNA), this is a general property of DNA and not specific to mitochondrial inheritance regulation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Polycistronic mRNA is characteristic of prokaryotes, mitochondria, some viruses, and in chloroplast in plants.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following statements regarding the structural organization of genetic material in human mitochondria is correct?
options: It is composed of closed, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules.
It contains only a single chromosome that is identical to the X chromosome.
It utilizes the same genetic code as nuclear DNA for all 64 codons.
It consists of linear DNA molecules associated with histone octamers.
It is inherited equally from both the maternal and paternal lines.
correctOption: It is composed of closed, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules.
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial DNA in humans consists of small, closed, circular, double-stranded molecules, similar in structure to prokaryotic plasmids.
Mitochondria have their own unique genome which is distinct from the 23 pairs of nuclear chromosomes (including the X chromosome).
The mitochondrial genetic code has slight variations; for example, UGA codes for tryptophan in mitochondria instead of acting as a stop codon.
Nuclear DNA is linear and associated with histones to form nucleosomes; mitochondrial DNA is circular and lacks histones.
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited exclusively from the mother (maternal inheritance) because the mitochondria in the zygote are derived from the ovum.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Eukaryotes have closed, circular, dsDNA molecules in their mitochondria

statement: In clinical genetics, what is the term for the first person in a family to be brought to the attention of a geneticist, often represented in a pedigree by an arrow?
options: Consanguineous
Proband
Genotype
Haploid
Allele
correctOption: Proband
optionExplanations: Consanguineous refers to a relationship between individuals who are closely related by blood.
The proband (or propositus/proposita) is the individual who first draws medical attention to a family's genetic condition.
Genotype is the genetic constitution of an individual organism.
Haploid refers to a cell or organism having a single set of unpaired chromosomes (n).
An allele is one of two or more alternative forms of a gene that arise by mutation and are found at the same place on a chromosome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent pulmonary infections, chronic cough, and foul-smelling, bulky stools. Laboratory testing reveals a high chloride concentration in the sweat. Molecular analysis shows a three-base deletion (delta-F508) in the CFTR gene. Which of the following best describes the fate of the resulting protein product in this patient?
options: It folds incorrectly and is targeted for destruction by the proteasome
It is trapped in the Golgi apparatus and converted into a different isoform
It is transcribed into a truncated mRNA that is rapidly degraded in the nucleus
It is successfully integrated into the membrane but cannot be phosphorylated
It is secreted normally but fails to bind chloride ions in the extracellular space
correctOption: It folds incorrectly and is targeted for destruction by the proteasome
optionExplanations: The delta-F508 mutation causes the CFTR protein to fold improperly; the cell's quality control system marks it with ubiquitin for degradation by the proteasome.
The protein is recognized as defective much earlier in the pathway, primarily in the endoplasmic reticulum, not the Golgi.
The delta-F508 is an in-frame deletion of one amino acid, not a nonsense mutation, so a full-length (minus one residue) protein is translated but then misfolds.
The majority of delta-F508 CFTR does not reach the plasma membrane; it is degraded intracellularly after failing the folding check.
The protein never reaches the cell membrane in the delta-F508 mutation, so extracellular binding is not the primary defect.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: When comparing the pedigrees of two distinct metabolic disorders, Disorder A shows affected siblings with unaffected parents, while Disorder B shows affected individuals in every generation. Which diagnostic contrast correctly identifies these patterns?
options: Disorder A is X-linked dominant; Disorder B is X-linked recessive.
Disorder A is autosomal recessive; Disorder B is autosomal dominant.
Disorder A is mitochondrial; Disorder B is autosomal recessive.
Disorder A is X-linked recessive; Disorder B is mitochondrial.
Disorder A is autosomal dominant; Disorder B is autosomal recessive.
correctOption: Disorder A is autosomal recessive; Disorder B is autosomal dominant.
optionExplanations: X-linked dominant traits do not skip generations like the 'affected siblings with normal parents' pattern seen in Disorder A.

Autosomal recessive (AR) traits often appear 'horizontally' in siblings of a single generation with carrier parents, whereas Autosomal dominant (AD) traits appear 'vertically' across multiple generations.
Mitochondrial traits are passed from a mother to all children, not just appearing in a horizontal sibship with normal parents.
X-linked recessive traits usually show a pattern where males are affected, but they do not typically appear in siblings of both sexes with the same frequency as autosomal recessive traits.
This reverses the descriptions provided in the stem; Disorder A fits the recessive pattern, not the dominant one.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (SLOS) is an embryonic malformation syndrome caused by a deficiency in 7-dehydrocholesterol-7-reductase. A couple, both of whom are healthy, have a child diagnosed with SLOS. What is the probability that their next child will also be affected by this specific biochemical defect?
optionExplanations: A 100% risk would require both parents to be homozygous for the recessive mutation.

SLOS is an autosomal recessive disorder. Since both parents are asymptomatic carriers (having already produced one affected child), there is a 1 in 4 (25%) chance for each subsequent pregnancy to result in an affected child.
The risk is not 0% because the parents are carriers of the recessive mutation.
A 50% risk would occur if one parent was affected and the other was a carrier, or in an autosomal dominant condition with one affected parent.

A 75% risk describes the probability of a child being unaffected (either healthy or a carrier) in an autosomal recessive cross, or being affected in a cross between two autosomal dominant heterozygotes.

coreConcept: ASO Probe Interpretation in AR Traits
statement: When using Allele-Specific Oligonucleotide (ASO) probes to diagnose Sickle Cell Anemia (an autosomal recessive trait), which result confirms that a patient is a carrier (heterozygous) rather than having the disease?
options: No binding occurs with either the normal or mutant probes.
The DNA fragment generated is 1.35 kb only.
Binding occurs only with the probe for the normal HbA allele.
Binding occurs with both the normal HbA and mutant HbS probes.
Binding occurs only with the probe for the mutant HbS allele.
correctOption: Binding occurs with both the normal HbA and mutant HbS probes.
optionExplanations: A lack of binding to either probe suggests a technical failure or a different mutation not covered by the ASO probes.
A 1.35 kb fragment on an MstII RFLP analysis indicates the loss of a restriction site, characteristic of the HbS allele; a carrier would show both 1.15 kb and 1.35 kb fragments.
Binding only to the normal probe indicates a homozygous normal genotype (non-carrier).
In an autosomal recessive carrier (heterozygote), one allele is normal and one is mutant. Therefore, the DNA will hybridize with both the normal-sequence probe and the mutant-sequence probe.
Binding only to the mutant probe indicates a homozygous mutant genotype (affected by Sickle Cell Anemia).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Use of a pair of such ASO probes (one specific for the normal allele and one specific for the mutant allele) allows all three possible genotypes (homozygous normal, heterozygous, and homozygous mutant) to be distinguished.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which characteristic feature differentiates X-linked dominant rickets from X-linked recessive disorders?
options: Affected mothers only pass the trait to their sons.
Affected fathers pass the trait to 50% of their sons.
Affected fathers pass the trait to all of their daughters.
It skips generations frequently.
It only affects males.
correctOption: Affected fathers pass the trait to all of their daughters.
optionExplanations: An affected mother (heterozygous) passes the X-linked dominant allele to 50% of her children, regardless of their sex.
Fathers never pass their X chromosome to their sons; they pass the Y chromosome, so sons of an affected father cannot inherit an X-linked trait from him.
A father provides his single X chromosome to all his daughters and his Y chromosome to all his sons; thus, all daughters of an affected father will receive the dominant trait.
Dominant traits (whether autosomal or X-linked) generally appear in every generation and do not skip unless there is incomplete penetrance.
X-linked dominant traits affect both males and females, often with females being more frequently affected but with milder symptoms.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": X-linked dominant (Rickets)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In mitochondrial inheritance, such as that seen in Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes (MELAS), why are these traits exclusively transmitted by the mother to her offspring?
options: Spermatozoa contain no mitochondria and thus cannot transmit mtDNA.
The Y chromosome suppresses the expression of paternal mitochondrial genes.
Paternal mitochondria are restricted to the head of the sperm which does not enter the egg.
The zygote inherits its entire complement of cytoplasm and organelles from the oocyte.
Mitochondrial DNA in the sperm is degraded by lysosomal enzymes in the fallopian tube.
correctOption: The zygote inherits its entire complement of cytoplasm and organelles from the oocyte.
optionExplanations: While sperm do have mitochondria for energy, they do not contribute them to the offspring; the premise that they have 'none' is biologically incorrect as they need energy for motility.
Mitochondrial DNA is extrachromosomal and its inheritance is not regulated or suppressed by the sex chromosomes (X or Y).
Mitochondrial DNA is concentrated in the midpiece of the sperm, not the head, and while the midpiece may enter, these paternal mitochondria are specifically targeted for destruction or diluted.

Mitochondrial inheritance follows a non-Mendelian pattern because the large oocyte provides the cytoplasm and all organelles (including mitochondria) to the zygote, while the sperm contributes only nuclear DNA.
There is no evidence of specific fallopian tube lysosomal degradation of sperm mtDNA; the primary reason is the lack of cytoplasmic contribution from the sperm to the zygote.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": DNA, the repository of genetic information (the genome), is present not only in chromosomes in the nucleus of eukaryotic organisms, but also in mitochondria... The human mitochondrial chromosome carries 22 tRNA genes.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which criterion is most characteristic of an autosomal dominant trait in a large, multi-generational human pedigree?
options: Affected individuals are almost exclusively male.
The trait is transmitted only from fathers to their sons.
The trait is only transmitted if both parents are symptomatic.
The trait appears only in individuals who are homozygous for the mutant allele.
Every affected individual typically has at least one affected parent.
correctOption: Every affected individual typically has at least one affected parent.
optionExplanations: This describes X-linked recessive inheritance; autosomal dominant traits affect males and females equally.
Father-to-son transmission of a nuclear trait suggests autosomal inheritance (if both sexes affected) or Y-linked; AD affects both sexes.
Only one parent needs to be symptomatic (heterozygous) to transmit an autosomal dominant trait to 50% of the offspring.
Autosomal dominant traits are expressed in heterozygotes (Aa), not just homozygotes (AA).
Correct. Autosomal dominant traits show vertical transmission, meaning every affected child usually has an affected parent in each generation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which genetic term refers to the condition of having only one representative of a chromosome or gene, such as the X chromosome in human males?
options: Hemizygous
Aneuploidy
Heterozygous
Homozygous
Codominance
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Hemizygous is the correct term for having only one copy of a gene or chromosome instead of the usual two; males are hemizygous for most genes on the X and Y chromosomes.
Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy), not the state of the alleles themselves.
Heterozygous refers to having two different alleles for a particular gene.
Homozygous refers to having two identical alleles for a particular gene on homologous chromosomes.
Codominance is a relationship between two versions of a gene where both alleles are expressed equally in the phenotype.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: X-linked Recessive Logic and Carrier Transmission
statement: In the study of a family pedigree, an elite examiner notices that a trait for Hemophilia A is never passed from an affected father to his sons, but all daughters of an affected father become obligate carriers. This observation confirms which pattern of inheritance?
options: Mitochondrial
X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
Holandric (Y-linked)
correctOption: X-linked recessive
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial inheritance involves maternal transmission only; an affected father does not pass the trait to any offspring.

In X-linked recessive inheritance, a father passes his only X chromosome (carrying the mutation) to all of his daughters, making them carriers. He passes his Y chromosome to his sons, ensuring they do not inherit the X-linked trait from him.
Autosomal dominant traits can be passed from father to son (male-to-male transmission), which is absent here.

Autosomal recessive traits would require the mother to also provide an allele for the daughter to be even a carrier; it doesn't result in all daughters being obligate carriers unless the father is affected.
Holandric traits are passed from father to all sons and no daughters, which is the exact opposite of the observed pattern.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: 1) X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following conditions is diagnosed based on an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance, where the defect involves the inability to repair DNA damage caused by ultraviolet radiation?
options: Xeroderma pigmentosum
Huntington disease
Familial hypercholesterolemia
Lynch syndrome
Severe combined immunodeficiency
correctOption: Xeroderma pigmentosum
optionExplanations: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is a classic autosomal recessive disorder. It is caused by mutations in genes required for nucleotide excision repair (NER), leading to an inability to repair pyrimidine dimers formed by UV exposure.
Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by triplet repeat expansions.
Familial hypercholesterolemia is an autosomal dominant disorder involving defects in the LDL receptor or apo B-100.
Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition resulting from mutations in DNA mismatch repair proteins (like MSH2 and MLH1).
While SCID is a genetic immune deficiency, the specific criteria for a DNA repair defect linked to UV sensitivity defines Xeroderma Pigmentosum (Objective 13).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": In the rare, human genetic disease xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), an individual’s skin cells cannot repair pyrimidine dimers caused by sunlight.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A couple has a child diagnosed with Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS). They are planning a second pregnancy. What is the calculated risk that their next child will be clinically affected by this specific disorder?
optionExplanations: The 50% risk would apply to the chance of the child being an asymptomatic carrier, or to a dominant trait with one affected heterozygous parent.
The risk is not 0% because both parents have already been proven to be carriers by having an affected child.
75% is the probability that the child will NOT be clinically affected (combining the 25% homozygous normal and 50% carrier probabilities).
For an autosomal recessive disorder like SLOS, each pregnancy between two carriers has a 25% (1 in 4) chance of resulting in an affected (homozygous recessive) child.
A 100% risk only occurs if both parents are homozygous for the recessive mutation, which is not the standard scenario for these rare metabolic syndromes.

statement: Which specific biochemical finding is a hallmark of the autosomal recessive disorder Cystic Fibrosis, specifically the ΔF508 mutation?
options: A point mutation causing the creation of a new MstII restriction site.
A cytosine-to-uracil deamination creating a premature stop codon.
A three-base deletion leading to the loss of a phenylalanine residue and subsequent proteasomal degradation.
The presence of extra G-rich tandem repeats at the ends of chromosomes.
A deficiency in the excision of pyrimidine dimers via the UvrABC complex.

optionExplanations: Incorrect. This point mutation describes the sickle cell allele, not CF.
Incorrect. This describes RNA editing of Apolipoprotein B in the intestine.
Correct. ΔF508 is a 3-bp deletion that removes Phenylalanine, causing protein misfolding and degradation by the proteasome.
Incorrect. This refers to telomeres and telomerase activity.
Incorrect. This describes the mechanism of Xeroderma Pigmentosum, not CF.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which specific chromosomal configuration is characteristic of a male patient affected by an X-linked recessive trait such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy?
options: He possesses two X chromosomes, both carrying the mutant allele.
He possesses a mutant allele on an autosome that is only expressed in the presence of testosterone.
He possesses two X chromosomes, one with the mutant allele and one normal.
He possesses three copies of the X chromosome (trisomy X).
He possesses a single X chromosome carrying the mutant allele and a Y chromosome.
correctOption: He possesses a single X chromosome carrying the mutant allele and a Y chromosome.
optionExplanations: This would describe an affected female (homozygous), which is rare for X-linked recessive traits.
This describes a sex-influenced autosomal trait, which is not the pattern for DMD.
This describes a carrier female (heterozygous), who is typically asymptomatic.
Trisomy X (XXX) is a numerical chromosomal abnormality, not the cause of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
Males are XY. In X-linked recessive disorders, a male is affected if his single X chromosome carries the mutation. This is known as the hemizygous state.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 28-year-old female presents with exercise intolerance, jerking muscle spasms, and lactic acidosis. Histological analysis of a muscle biopsy reveals 'ragged red fibers.' Her mother and maternal grandmother also suffered from progressive muscle weakness. What is the most likely mode of inheritance for this patient's condition?
options: Mitochondrial inheritance due to tRNA mutations.
Autosomal dominant with variable expressivity.
X-linked recessive with skewed X-inactivation.
Germline mosaicism in the maternal line.
Autosomal recessive involving mitochondrial protein transport.
correctOption: Mitochondrial inheritance due to tRNA mutations.
optionExplanations: Correct. MERRF and MELAS are mitochondrial diseases. They are characterized by 'ragged red fibers' (aggregates of abnormal mitochondria) and are inherited exclusively through the mother. The mutations often occur in mitochondrial tRNA genes.
Autosomal dominant traits show vertical transmission but do not typically show the maternal-only restriction or the specific 'ragged red fiber' pathology associated with mitochondrial DNA.

X-linked recessive traits primarily affect males. Females are usually carriers. While skewed X-inactivation can cause symptoms, the pedigree described (mother and grandmother affected) fits the maternal line transmission of mitochondria.
Germline mosaicism explains the appearance of a trait in multiple siblings of unaffected parents, not the continuous maternal line transmission seen here.
While some mitochondrial proteins are encoded by the nucleus (autosomal), the classic presentation of MERRF with maternal inheritance points to the mitochondrial genome itself.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A male is described as 'hemizygous' regarding a specific gene locus. Which of the following best describes the inheritance implication of this term?
options: The gene is located on an autosome and he has two different alleles.
The gene is located on the X chromosome and he has only one copy.
The gene has been amplified into multiple copies through transposition.
The gene is located on an autosome and both alleles are identical.
The gene is located in the mitochondria and is inherited from his father.
correctOption: The gene is located on the X chromosome and he has only one copy.
optionExplanations: A person with two different alleles on an autosome is called a heterozygote.
Hemizygous refers to having only one copy of a gene in a diploid cell. In males, this applies to most genes on the X and Y chromosomes.
Gene amplification increases copy number, whereas hemizygosity refers to the existence of only a single copy.
A person with two identical alleles on an autosome is called a homozygote.
Mitochondrial genes are hemizygous in a sense, but they are inherited exclusively from the mother, not the father.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: Autosomal Dominant Inheritance in Lipid Disorders
statement: Which of the following conditions is explicitly described as an autosomal dominant disorder that leads to premature atherosclerosis due to defects in the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor?
options: Niemann–Pick disease, type C
Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (SLOS)
Tangier disease
Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)
Wolman disease
correctOption: Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)
optionExplanations: Niemann–Pick disease, type C is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by a defect in transporting free cholesterol out of the lysosome.
Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome is characterized as an autosomal-recessive disorder involving cholesterol biosynthesis, not autosomal dominant.
Tangier disease is a very rare autosomal recessive deficiency of the ABCA1 transporter protein, resulting in the virtual absence of HDL particles.

Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is the definitive example of an autosomal dominant trait where even a single mutant allele for the LDL receptor or apo B-100 results in clinical disease and vascular risk.
Wolman disease is described as a rare autosomal-recessive deficiency in the ability to hydrolyze lysosomal cholesteryl esters.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: When comparing the transmission patterns of Mitochondrial disorders and X-linked dominant traits, what is the most reliable diagnostic contrast seen in the offspring of an affected father?
options: Affected fathers pass mitochondrial traits to all sons but no daughters
Mitochondrial traits are passed from an affected father only to his daughters
Mitochondrial traits are passed from an affected father to 50% of his offspring
X-linked dominant traits are passed from an affected father to all of his daughters
X-linked dominant traits are passed from an affected father to all of his sons
correctOption: X-linked dominant traits are passed from an affected father to all of his daughters
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial DNA is not transmitted by males; an affected father will not pass the trait to any of his children, regardless of sex.
Mitochondrial disorders are never passed by a father to his daughters; they are only inherited from the mother's oocyte.
Mitochondrial inheritance is strictly maternal; paternal mitochondria are not contributed to the zygote, resulting in zero transmission from fathers.
In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father provides his only X chromosome (carrying the mutation) to all his daughters, making them all affected.
A father passes his Y chromosome to his sons; since the mutation is on the X chromosome, he cannot pass an X-linked dominant trait to his sons.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA. Which feature of mitochondrial genetics explains why different family members may show widely varying degrees of symptom severity?
options: The presence of introns that are spliced differently in various tissues
The high rate of homologous recombination between mitochondrial and nuclear DNA
The degree of methylation on the mitochondrial promoter regions
The phenomenon of heteroplasmy, where a cell contains a mix of normal and mutant DNA
The different number of X chromosomes present in the affected individuals
correctOption: The phenomenon of heteroplasmy, where a cell contains a mix of normal and mutant DNA
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial DNA is very compact and generally lacks the complex intron-exon structures found in nuclear DNA.
Mitochondrial DNA is replicated independently and does not undergo significant homologous recombination with nuclear DNA.
While epigenetics exists, heteroplasmy is the primary determinant of phenotypic variation in mitochondrial DNA mutations.
Heteroplasmy refers to the mixture of mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA within a single cell; the severity of disease depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria (threshold effect).
Mitochondrial inheritance is independent of the sex chromosomes; it follows a non-Mendelian maternal pattern.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: When interpreting a pedigree for a suspected autosomal recessive trait, the presence of which of the following increases the probability of seeing the phenotype in the offspring of phenotypically normal parents?
options: Maternal age over 35
Hemizygosity
Heteroplasmy
Consanguinity
Vertical transmission
correctOption: Consanguinity
optionExplanations: Advanced maternal age is primarily a risk factor for chromosomal nondisjunction (aneuploidy), not for the inheritance of single-gene autosomal recessive traits.
Hemizygosity is the state of having only one copy of a gene (as in males for X-linked genes) and does not apply to autosomal recessive inheritance where two alleles are present.
Heteroplasmy refers to the presence of more than one type of organellar genome (mitochondrial DNA) within a cell and is relevant only to mitochondrial inheritance.

Consanguinity (mating between close relatives) increases the likelihood that both parents have inherited the same rare recessive allele from a common ancestor, thus increasing the risk of autosomal recessive offspring.
Vertical transmission is a hallmark of dominant traits, whereas recessive traits often appear horizontally (in siblings).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In a physiological study of metabolic pathways, it is observed that a certain deficiency of an enzyme in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway manifests only when an individual possesses two non-functional alleles. This regulation of the metabolic pool via inheritance is a classic example of which pattern?
options: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy
Negative feedback loop of hormones
X-linked dominant inheritance
Autosomal recessive inheritance
Autosomal dominant inheritance
correctOption: Autosomal recessive inheritance
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy refers to a mix of normal and mutated mitochondrial DNA within a cell, not the interaction of two nuclear alleles.
While hormones regulate pathways via feedback, the specific requirement of 'two non-functional alleles' refers to genetic inheritance patterns.
X-linked dominant traits manifest even when only one mutated allele is present (in females) or the single X is mutated (in males).

In many metabolic pathways, a single functional allele (heterozygous state) produces enough enzyme to maintain a normal physiological state. Thus, the disease only manifests when both alleles are non-functional, which is the definition of autosomal recessive inheritance.
Autosomal dominant traits manifest with only one non-functional (or gain-of-function) allele.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the context of X-linked recessive inheritance, which mechanism best explains why these traits typically manifest in males and skip generations through the maternal line?
options: Affected fathers pass the trait to all of their sons but none of their daughters.
A single mutant X chromosome in males is sufficient for expression due to the lack of a second X allele.
Males require two copies of the mutant allele to express the phenotype.
The trait is only passed from father to son via the Y chromosome.
Females are hemizygous for the X chromosome, making them more susceptible.
correctOption: A single mutant X chromosome in males is sufficient for expression due to the lack of a second X allele.
optionExplanations: Affected fathers pass their single X chromosome to all daughters (making them carriers) but never to their sons, who receive the Y chromosome from the father.
Because males have only one X chromosome, they cannot mask a recessive mutant allele with a dominant wild-type allele, leading to full phenotypic expression of the trait.
In X-linked recessive traits, males only need one copy, while females usually require two copies (homozygosity) to express the phenotype.
Y-linked inheritance (holandric) involves the Y chromosome, but X-linked recessive traits are located on the X chromosome and passed from carrier mothers to sons.
Males, not females, are hemizygous for the X chromosome because they possess only one X and one Y chromosome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 40-year-old male presents with chorea and progressive cognitive impairment. His father exhibited similar symptoms before dying at age 48. Genetic analysis confirms Huntington disease. What is the probability that his unborn son will develop this condition?
options: 100% because the father is already symptomatic.
75% because males are more likely to inherit the expansion from their fathers.
50% because the condition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
0% if the mother does not carry the mutation.
25% as the child must inherit alleles from both parents.
correctOption: 50% because the condition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Even if the father is symptomatic, he still only has a 50% chance of passing the specific mutant allele to his child.
Incorrect. The risk for an autosomal dominant trait is 50% per pregnancy. While 'anticipation' can occur in triplet repeat expansions, the basic Mendelian probability remains 50%.

Correct. Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder. An affected individual is typically a heterozygote (Hh). When paired with a normal individual (hh), there is a 50% probability (Hh or hh) for each child to inherit the mutant allele and eventually develop the disease.
Incorrect. In autosomal dominant disorders like Huntington disease, only one parent needs to carry the mutation to pass it to the offspring.
Incorrect. 25% is the risk for autosomal recessive traits when both parents are carriers. Huntington's is dominant.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: An elite medical board examiner asks a student to define the term used to describe the genotype of a male for genes located on the X chromosome. What is the correct term?
options: Hemizygous
Heterozygous
Aneuploid
Homozygous
Haploid
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Hemizygous describes the state of having only one copy of a particular gene or chromosome instead of the usual two. Males are hemizygous for most genes on the sex chromosomes because they have only one X and one Y.
Heterozygous means having two different alleles for a particular gene, which is also impossible for X-linked genes in a normal male.
Aneuploid refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell (e.g., trisomy), not the standard genotype of a male for X-linked genes.
Homozygous means having two identical alleles for a particular gene, which is impossible for X-linked genes in a normal male.
Haploid refers to a cell having a single set of unpaired chromosomes (like a sperm or egg cell), not the genotype of a somatic cell.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: RNA Interference in Dominant Genetic Disease
statement: A patient with hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR), an autosomal dominant condition, is prescribed patisiran. Which mechanism describes how this drug targets the gene expression pattern characteristic of this inheritance?
options: It acts as a competitive inhibitor of the transthyretin protein's enzymatic active site.
It promotes the methylation of the TTR promoter to silence the mutant allele exclusively.
It binds to the mutant DNA to prevent its replication during the S phase.
It facilitates the recruitment of chaperones to the rough endoplasmic reticulum to refold the mutant TTR.
It utilizes the RNA interference pathway to degrade transthyretin mRNA, reducing the levels of the pathogenic protein.
correctOption: It utilizes the RNA interference pathway to degrade transthyretin mRNA, reducing the levels of the pathogenic protein.
optionExplanations: Transthyretin is a transport protein, not an enzyme. Patisiran reduces its synthesis rather than inhibiting its function via a binding site.
Patisiran does not induce DNA methylation; it works post-transcriptionally by targeting mRNA in the cytosol.
Patisiran is an siRNA-based drug that acts in the cytoplasm on mRNA, not on the DNA in the nucleus during replication.
While misfolded proteins can trigger a chaperone response, patisiran's mechanism is to prevent the synthesis of the protein entirely by silencing the mRNA, rather than attempting to refold it.

Correct. Patisiran uses small interfering RNA (siRNA) to trigger the RNA interference (RNAi) pathway. By degrading the mRNA of both the mutant and wild-type TTR, it prevents the synthesis of the toxic, amyloid-forming protein that causes the dominant phenotype.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A clinician is evaluating two different families. In Family A, an affected father has all affected daughters and no affected sons. In Family B, an affected father has no affected children, but his daughters' sons are often affected. What are the most likely modes of inheritance for the traits in Family A and Family B, respectively?
options: Family A: X-linked recessive; Family B: X-linked dominant
Family A: Autosomal dominant; Family B: Autosomal recessive
Family A: X-linked dominant; Family B: X-linked recessive
Family A: Mitochondrial; Family B: Y-linked
Family A: Autosomal recessive; Family B: Mitochondrial
correctOption: Family A: X-linked dominant; Family B: X-linked recessive
optionExplanations: In X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected father cannot have affected daughters unless the mother is a carrier. In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father must have affected daughters.
In autosomal dominant traits, an affected father can pass the trait to his sons. In autosomal recessive traits, an affected father's children would only be affected if the mother is also a carrier.

In Family A, the father passes the trait to all daughters (who receive his X) but no sons (who receive his Y), defining X-linked dominant. In Family B, the father passes the allele to daughters who are unaffected carriers, but they pass it to their sons, defining X-linked recessive.
Mitochondrial traits are never passed by a father. Y-linked traits are passed from a father to all his sons, which contradicts the observation in Family B.

Autosomal recessive would require both parents to be affected or carriers to show the phenotype in children. Mitochondrial traits only show transmission from the mother's side, never the father's side as seen in Family A's affected father description (if he were to pass it).

statement: Which of the following describes the most distinctive feature of mitochondrial inheritance?
options: The trait skips generations and is associated with consanguinity.
Male and female offspring have a 50% chance of inheriting the trait from an affected father.
Traits are only expressed in individuals who are hemizygous.
Traits are passed from affected fathers to all their daughters.
Offspring of an affected male are never affected.
correctOption: Offspring of an affected male are never affected.
optionExplanations: Skipping generations and association with consanguinity are classic features of autosomal recessive inheritance.
A 50% chance of inheritance from an affected father is characteristic of autosomal dominant traits.
Hemizygosity is a characteristic of X-linked inheritance in males, not mitochondrial inheritance.
Affected fathers passing to all daughters is the hallmark of X-linked dominant inheritance.
Mitochondrial inheritance is strictly maternal. Therefore, an affected male cannot transmit the mitochondria (and thus the trait) to any of his children.

statement: A family presents with a child affected by Phenylketonuria (PKU). Southern blot analysis using a PAH-cDNA probe reveals that the mutant allele in this family is associated with a 1.35-kb restriction fragment, while the normal allele is associated with a 1.15-kb fragment. The mother is currently pregnant. If fetal DNA shows only the 1.35-kb fragment, what is the diagnosis and biochemical basis?
options: The fetus is a carrier; one restriction site was lost.
The fetus has a chromosomal translocation of the PAH gene.
The fetus is affected; both alleles lack a specific restriction site, indicating biallelic mutation.
The fetus is affected; the fragment size is irrelevant to the inheritance pattern.
The fetus is healthy; the larger fragment indicates increased enzyme production.
correctOption: The fetus is affected; both alleles lack a specific restriction site, indicating biallelic mutation.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. A carrier would show both the 1.15-kb and 1.35-kb bands (heterozygous).
Incorrect. A translocation would change the location, but RFLP analysis here specifically tracks the inheritance of specific alleles via fragment size.

Correct. Since the parents have an affected child, they are both carriers. The 1.35-kb fragment marks the mutant allele. If the fetus shows only the 1.35-kb band, it is homozygous for the mutation and thus affected.
Incorrect. The fragment size is the primary marker used to distinguish the inheritance of the mutant vs. normal allele in this linkage analysis.
Incorrect. Fragment size in Southern blotting relates to DNA sequence/restriction sites, not the 'amount' or 'speed' of enzyme production.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In genetic nomenclature, which term refers to the specific physical location of a gene on a chromosome, and which term describes an individual having two identical alleles at that location?
options: Proband; Heterozygote
Genotype; Phenotype
Locus; Heterozygote
Locus; Homozygote
Allele; Homozygote
correctOption: Locus; Homozygote
optionExplanations: A proband is the first affected individual in a family brought to medical attention; a heterozygote has different alleles.
Genotype is the genetic makeup, and phenotype is the observable physical trait; neither defines a specific chromosomal location.
Locus is the correct term for location, but a heterozygote has two different alleles, not identical ones.
A 'locus' is the specific site on a chromosome where a gene is found, and a 'homozygote' is an individual possessing two identical alleles at a given locus.
An allele is a variant form of a gene, not its location.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the context of X-linked recessive disorders such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, which physiological principle explains why males are more frequently affected than females?
options: Maternal imprinting of the paternal X chromosome
Presence of the SRY gene on the X chromosome
X-chromosome inactivation (Lyonization) in males
Somatic recombination of the dystrophin gene
Male hemizygosity for the X chromosome
correctOption: Male hemizygosity for the X chromosome
optionExplanations: Imprinting involves the epigenetic silencing of specific genes based on parental origin, but the classic high frequency of X-linked recessive traits in males is due to the simple lack of a second X chromosome.
The SRY gene is located on the Y chromosome, not the X chromosome, and is responsible for male sex determination, not the manifestation of X-linked recessive diseases.
X-chromosome inactivation occurs in females to balance the dosage of X-linked genes; males have only one X chromosome and do not undergo Lyonization.
Somatic recombination is a process used in the generation of immunoglobulin diversity but is not the standard mechanism for the inheritance or manifestation of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.

Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes because they possess only one X chromosome. Therefore, a single mutant allele on the X chromosome is sufficient to cause the phenotype, as there is no corresponding allele on the Y chromosome to provide a functional product.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In mitochondrial disorders like MERRF, why might different members of the same family exhibit varying degrees of clinical severity despite inheriting the same maternal mutation?
options: Incomplete penetrance of autosomal alleles
Heteroplasmy and the threshold effect
Variable splicing of the mitochondrial mRNA
Presence of a second-site suppressor on the Y chromosome
Varying degrees of X-inactivation
correctOption: Heteroplasmy and the threshold effect
optionExplanations: MERRF is a mitochondrial disorder, not an autosomal one, so autosomal penetrance rules do not define its primary variance.

Heteroplasmy refers to the mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA within a cell. Clinical severity depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria inherited; a higher proportion must be present (threshold effect) to cause severe disease.
While splicing occurs in the nucleus, the variation in mitochondrial disease severity is most fundamentally linked to the ratio of mutant-to-normal DNA molecules (heteroplasmy).
Mitochondrial DNA is not influenced by Y-chromosome genes in the manner described for typical phenotypic variation.
X-inactivation affects genes on the X chromosome; mitochondrial DNA is extranuclear and independent of X-chromosome dynamics.

statement: Which of the following medical conditions is classified as an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by neurodegeneration and triplet repeat expansion?
options: Mitochondrial diabetes
Cystic Fibrosis
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
Xeroderma Pigmentosum
Huntington’s Disease
correctOption: Huntington’s Disease
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial diabetes follows a mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance pattern, where the trait is passed only through the mother to all her children.
Cystic Fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, requiring both parents to be carriers for a child to be affected.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder, not autosomal dominant, affecting primarily males through carrier mothers.
Xeroderma Pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive condition involving defective nucleotide excision repair, requiring two mutant alleles for phenotypic expression.
Huntington's Disease is a classic autosomal dominant disorder where a single mutant allele on an autosome is sufficient to cause the disease, often involving triplet repeat expansions.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A male patient with Vitamin D-resistant Rickets, an X-linked dominant disorder, seeks genetic counseling. He is concerned about the risk of passing the condition to his children. Which of the following transmission patterns is expected for this patient's offspring?
options: None of his children will be affected as he is hemizygous.
Only his daughters will be carriers, showing no phenotypic symptoms.
All of his daughters will be affected, but none of his sons.
All of his sons will be affected, but none of his daughters.
There is a 50% chance for each child to be affected regardless of sex.
correctOption: All of his daughters will be affected, but none of his sons.
optionExplanations: Hemizygosity in the father means he has the mutation on his only X chromosome, which ensures transmission to specific offspring (daughters).
In X-linked dominant conditions, a single copy of the mutant gene is sufficient to cause the disease; hence daughters will be affected patients, not asymptomatic carriers.

In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father passes his only X chromosome (carrying the mutation) to all of his daughters, who will then express the phenotype. He passes his Y chromosome to all his sons.
Sons of an affected father receive his Y chromosome, not his X chromosome; therefore, an affected father cannot pass an X-linked trait to his sons.
A 50% risk for all children is characteristic of an affected mother, who can pass either the normal or the mutant X chromosome. A father's transmission is sex-dependent.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: AD vs AR Inheritance of Metabolic Disorders
statement: Patisiran, a small interfering RNA (siRNA) based drug, is used to treat hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR). Since this is a 'hereditary' condition caused by a single-gene mutation, how does its typical transmission pattern differ from that of Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency?
options: hATTR is typically autosomal dominant (requiring one mutant allele), while ADA deficiency is autosomal recessive (requiring two).
hATTR is autosomal recessive, while ADA deficiency is autosomal dominant.
hATTR is X-linked recessive, while ADA deficiency is mitochondrial.
hATTR is mitochondrial, while ADA deficiency is X-linked dominant.
hATTR is X-linked dominant, while ADA deficiency is X-linked recessive.
correctOption: hATTR is typically autosomal dominant (requiring one mutant allele), while ADA deficiency is autosomal recessive (requiring two).
optionExplanations: In medical genetics, hATTR is a well-known autosomal dominant condition where a mutation in one allele of the TTR gene causes amyloid buildup. Conversely, ADA-deficient SCID is a classic autosomal recessive disorder (as noted in common biochemistry contexts and gene therapy chapters), requiring inheritance of two defective alleles for the disease to manifest.
This reverses the typical patterns for these two specific conditions.
The text lists ADA deficiency as a target for somatic gene therapy but does not classify it as mitochondrial. Mitochondrial disorders like MERRF involve tRNA mutations.
HATTR is not mitochondrial; it is nuclear. ADA deficiency is not X-linked dominant; it is autosomal.
HATTR and ADA deficiency are both autosomal, not X-linked.

statement: A patient is diagnosed with a metabolic disorder characterized by muscle spasms and 'ragged red fibers' on biopsy. The patient’s mother and all three of her siblings (two brothers and one sister) show similar neurological symptoms, but her father is completely healthy. What is the most likely inheritance pattern and underlying mechanism for this trait?
options: Autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.
X-linked dominant with male lethality.
Mitochondrial inheritance involving maternal transmission.
X-linked recessive with skewed lyonization.
Autosomal recessive due to a shared environmental toxin.
correctOption: Mitochondrial inheritance involving maternal transmission.
optionExplanations: Autosomal dominant would likely show transmission from either parent, not just the mother to all her children.
X-linked dominant with male lethality would result in no living affected brothers and frequent miscarriages in the mother's history.
Mitochondrial disorders like MERRF are transmitted only by females to all their offspring because mitochondria are inherited solely from the oocyte. The father never passes these traits.
X-linked recessive would rarely affect a sister to the same degree as her brothers in a single generation unless she was homozygous.
Autosomal recessive would typically affect only 25% of siblings and would not explain why all children of the affected mother are symptomatic.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following descriptions best defines the characteristic pattern of autosomal recessive inheritance in a human pedigree?
options: The trait is transmitted only from an affected father to all of his sons.
The trait is found in approximately 75% of the offspring of two unaffected parents.
The trait is expressed only if the mother is affected and she passes it to all her children.
The trait often appears in siblings (horizontal pattern) but not in their parents.
The trait is expressed only in males and is passed from an affected father to his grandsons.
correctOption: The trait often appears in siblings (horizontal pattern) but not in their parents.
optionExplanations: This describes Y-linked (holandric) inheritance, which is not the pattern for autosomal recessive traits.
In a cross between two carriers, 75% is the probability of the offspring being unaffected (25% homozygous normal + 50% carrier), not affected.
This describes mitochondrial inheritance, where the phenotype is strictly dependent on the maternal genotype.

Autosomal recessive traits are characterized by a horizontal pattern, where the disease may appear in several members of a single sibship while the parents and subsequent generations appear unaffected, as both parents must be carriers.
This describes the pattern of X-linked recessive inheritance with 'generation skipping' via carrier females; autosomal recessive traits affect both sexes equally.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following terms is used to describe the situation where an individual possesses only one copy of a gene or chromosome, such as a male for any gene located on the X chromosome?
options: Aneuploidy
Polygenic
Homozygote
Heterozygote
Hemizygous
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy), not the state of the alleles on a single chromosome.
Polygenic refers to a trait controlled by multiple genes at different loci, rather than a single gene state.
A homozygote has two identical alleles (AA or aa) at a specific locus.
A heterozygote has two different alleles (Aa) at a specific locus on homologous chromosomes.
Hemizygous refers to having only one copy of a particular gene. This is the normal state for genes on the X and Y chromosomes in human males.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following inheritance patterns is most characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), where males are primarily affected and females serve as asymptomatic carriers?
options: Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial inheritance
X-linked dominant
Autosomal dominant
correctOption: X-linked recessive
optionExplanations: Autosomal recessive inheritance requires two copies of the mutant gene and typically affects siblings in one generation without a sex bias.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a classic X-linked recessive disorder; the gene is located on the X chromosome, so males (who have only one X) are affected if they inherit the mutation, while females with one mutation are typically unaffected carriers.
Mitochondrial inheritance is characterized by transmission only through the maternal line to all offspring, regardless of sex, which differs from the pattern seen in DMD.
X-linked dominant traits would affect both males and females, and an affected father would pass the trait to all of his daughters, which is not the case in DMD.
Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation and affect both sexes equally, which does not match the sex-biased distribution of DMD.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": A 4-year-old child who easily tires and has trouble walking is diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which molecular feature is common to mitochondrial inheritance disorders like MELAS and MERRF?
options: They are caused by point mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes.
They involve CAG repeat expansions in nuclear DNA.
They are inherited from the father through the Y chromosome.
They result from large deletions in the dystrophin gene.
They are characterized by a 50% recurrence risk from an affected father.
correctOption: They are caused by point mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes.
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS and MERRF are frequently caused by mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes, which impair mitochondrial protein synthesis.
CAG expansions in nuclear DNA are the hallmark of Huntington's disease (Autosomal Dominant).
Mitochondrial genes are inherited from the mother, not the father via the Y chromosome.
Large deletions in the dystrophin gene cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder.
Affected fathers do not transmit mitochondrial traits; the recurrence risk from an affected father is effectively 0%.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Mutations in the mitochondrial gene for tRNA Lys are associated with... MERRF... MELAS is also caused by mutations in the mitochondrial tRNA Leu gene.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following terms describes the chromosomal location and standard Mendelian requirement for an autosomal dominant trait to manifest its phenotype?
options: On a non-sex chromosome; requires two copies.
On the Y chromosome; affects only males.
On a non-sex chromosome; requires only one copy.
On a sex chromosome; requires two copies.
In the mitochondrial matrix; requires maternal transmission.
correctOption: On a non-sex chromosome; requires only one copy.
optionExplanations: Requiring two copies on an autosome describes autosomal recessive inheritance, not dominant.
Y-linked inheritance is restricted to males and does not involve autosomes or the standard dominant/recessive definitions applied to autosomes.
Autosomal dominant traits are located on autosomes (chromosomes 1-22) and manifest the phenotype in the heterozygous state (one mutant allele).
Autosomal traits are located on non-sex chromosomes (autosomes), and dominant traits require only one copy to manifest.
Mitochondrial matrix traits follow mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance, not autosomal dominant rules.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Autosome... dominant... Autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia can also be caused by defects in apo B-100

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A patient with a family history of premature atherosclerosis is found to have a genetic variant in the SLCO1B1 gene. This variant is known to increase the risk of myopathy when the patient is prescribed certain cholesterol-lowering drugs. What does this specific pharmacological interaction illustrate about genetic traits?
options: A trisomy-related defect in hepatic detoxification.
An autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance in all ethnic groups.
A mitochondrial trait affecting oxidative phosphorylation.
A genetic polymorphism influencing physiological response to medication.
An X-linked dominant trait involving drug transporters.
correctOption: A genetic polymorphism influencing physiological response to medication.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is a single nucleotide variation, not a chromosomal numerical abnormality like trisomy.
Incorrect. Polymorphisms do not imply 100% penetrance of a 'disease'; they signify a variable response to an environmental trigger (the drug).
Incorrect. While statin myopathy may involve mitochondria (Heme A/Ubiquinone inhibition), the SLCO1B1 variant is an autosomal polymorphism.
Correct. This is a classic example of a polymorphism (a sequence variation present in >1% of the population) affecting how a drug is transported and metabolized.
Incorrect. SLCO1B1 is not X-linked; it is located on an autosome.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Genetic polymorphisms also influence the physiologic response to statins. For example, organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP1B1, also known as SLCO1B1) has a polymorphism at nucleotide 521 T>C that is used as a biomarker for simvastatin myopathy.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: During a pedigree analysis, a student observes that an affected mother has passed a metabolic disorder to all her children, regardless of their sex. However, her affected son has only healthy children. This pattern is diagnostic of which inheritance type?
options: Autosomal dominant
Mitochondrial inheritance
X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
Autosomal recessive
correctOption: Mitochondrial inheritance
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Autosomal dominant traits can be passed from fathers to children; here, the father fails to pass the trait.
Correct. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited strictly from the mother via the oocyte cytoplasm. An affected male cannot pass the trait because sperm do not contribute mitochondria to the zygote.
Incorrect. Affected fathers with X-linked dominant traits must pass the trait to all their daughters; here, the father has healthy children.
Incorrect. In X-linked recessive, a mother would pass the trait only to her sons (if she is homozygous) or 50% of sons (if heterozygous); she wouldn't necessarily affect all children.
Incorrect. Recessive traits typically skip generations and do not affect 100% of offspring from one parent unless both parents are carriers.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Mitochondrial disorder (Mitochondrial diabetes). DNA is present not only in chromosomes in the nucleus of eukaryotic organisms, but also in mitochondria.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the case of Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (SLOS), an autosomal recessive disorder of cholesterol biosynthesis, what is the expected clinical status of the parents of an affected child?
options: One parent must be symptomatic, while the other is homozygous normal.
Both parents must be symptomatic to produce an affected child.
Both parents are typically asymptomatic carriers of the 7-dehydrocholesterol-7-reductase deficiency.
The father must be symptomatic, as the gene is located on the Y chromosome.
The mother must be symptomatic, as the gene is located on the X chromosome.
correctOption: Both parents are typically asymptomatic carriers of the 7-dehydrocholesterol-7-reductase deficiency.
optionExplanations: In autosomal recessive inheritance, parents are usually asymptomatic carriers (heterozygotes).
Symptomatic parents in a recessive trait would imply they are both homozygous (aa x aa), which is rare; most cases arise from asymptomatic carriers (Aa x Aa).
Correct. Autosomal recessive disorders manifest when an individual inherits two mutant alleles; therefore, both parents must at least be carriers.
SLOS is autosomal, not Y-linked.
SLOS is autosomal, meaning it is located on a non-sex chromosome, not the X chromosome.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (SLOS), an autosomal- recessive disorder of cholesterol biosynthesis, is caused by a partial deficiency in 7- dehydrocholesterol-7-reductase.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 5-year-old boy is diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) after presenting with Gowers' sign and pseudohypertrophy of the calves. His sister is unaffected. Which inheritance pattern describes this condition?
options: Mitochondrial
Autosomal Recessive
X-linked Recessive
X-linked Dominant
Autosomal Dominant
correctOption: X-linked Recessive
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial inheritance would result in all children of an affected mother being affected, which is not the pattern seen in DMD pedigrees.
While recessive, DMD is linked specifically to the X chromosome, meaning it affects males who receive one mutant X from their mother.

DMD is a classic X-linked recessive disorder. Males are primarily affected because they have only one X chromosome (hemizygous). Females are typically asymptomatic carriers because they have a second, normal X chromosome.
In X-linked dominant traits, the sister and the mother would likely also be affected, as one mutant allele would cause the phenotype.
Autosomal dominant traits would likely show an affected parent and would not be predominantly restricted to males as DMD is.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: 1) X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following descriptions best distinguishes the inheritance pattern of Autosomal Dominant Hypercholesterolemia from Autosomal Recessive disorders like Sickle Cell Anemia?
options: Autosomal dominant inheritance is only transmitted through the maternal line.
Autosomal dominant traits usually appear in every generation, whereas recessive traits may skip generations.
Autosomal dominant traits require two mutant alleles for phenotypic expression.
Autosomal dominant traits only affect males, while recessive traits affect both sexes.
Autosomal recessive traits are always visible in the phenotype of a heterozygote.
correctOption: Autosomal dominant traits usually appear in every generation, whereas recessive traits may skip generations.
optionExplanations: Maternal-only transmission is a hallmark of mitochondrial inheritance, not autosomal dominant inheritance.

Autosomal dominant traits typically show vertical transmission (appearing in every generation), while autosomal recessive traits often show horizontal transmission (appearing in siblings but not their parents), often appearing to skip generations.
Autosomal dominant traits express their phenotype with only one mutant allele (heterozygous state), whereas recessive traits require two.
Both autosomal dominant and recessive traits affect males and females with equal frequency because the genes are located on non-sex chromosomes.
In autosomal recessive inheritance, the heterozygote is an asymptomatic carrier and does not express the disease phenotype.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Patients with such deficiencies have type IIa hyperlipidemia [familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)] and premature atherosclerosis. Autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia can also be caused by defects in apo B-100 that reduce its binding to the receptor.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which term describes a single copy of a gene in a diploid cell, specifically referring to the X-linked genes in a male?
options: Heterozygous
Homozygous
Haploid
Aneuploid
Hemizygous
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Heterozygous refers to having two different alleles for a particular gene on homologous chromosomes.
Homozygous refers to having two identical alleles for a particular gene on homologous chromosomes.
Haploid refers to a cell having a single set of unpaired chromosomes (e.g., gametes), whereas the term for the gene state in a diploid male is hemizygous.
Aneuploid refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., 45 or 47 instead of 46) and does not describe the allelic state of a single gene.
Hemizygous describes the situation where only one copy of a gene is present in an otherwise diploid cell. This is the standard state for X-linked genes in males.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: Molecular Basis of Anticipation in Autosomal Dominant Traits
statement: Which genetic phenomenon, characteristic of Huntington Disease, explains why the age of onset may decrease and the severity of symptoms may increase in successive generations?
options: Somatic recombination
Variable penetrance
Epigenetic silencing
Trinucleotide repeat expansion
Locus heterogeneity
correctOption: Trinucleotide repeat expansion
optionExplanations: Somatic recombination is a process used by B-lymphocytes to generate antibody diversity, not a mechanism for inherited neurodegenerative disease.
Penetrance refers to whether the trait is expressed at all, not the worsening of symptoms or earlier onset across generations.

Epigenetic silencing (like DNA methylation) usually reduces gene expression and is associated with conditions like Fragile X syndrome or X-inactivation, rather than the gain-of-function seen in Huntington disease.

Huntington disease is caused by trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansions. These repeats can further expand during gametogenesis, leading to earlier onset and more severe disease in offspring, a process known as anticipation.
Locus heterogeneity occurs when mutations at different gene loci produce the same phenotype; it does not explain the generational change in a single family.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": expansion of the CAG codon in exon 1 of the gene for huntingtin protein leads to the insertion of many extra glutamine residues in the protein, causing the neurodegenerative disorder Huntington disease

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Vitamin D-resistant rickets is classified as an X-linked dominant trait. In a pedigree where the father is affected and the mother is phenotypically normal, what is the expected outcome for their children?
options: All children will be asymptomatic carriers
50% of the daughters will be affected
All daughters will be affected
50% of the sons will be affected
All sons will be affected
correctOption: All daughters will be affected
optionExplanations: X-linked dominant traits do not have 'asymptomatic carriers' in the traditional sense, as a single dose of the dominant allele produces the phenotype.
100% of the daughters will be affected because they receive the father's only X chromosome; the 50% probability only applies if the mother is the affected (heterozygous) parent.
An affected father (XDY) must pass his only X chromosome (which carries the dominant mutation) to all of his daughters, making 100% of them affected.
Sons of an affected father and a normal mother will never inherit the X-linked trait because they receive only the Y chromosome from the father.
In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father (XDY) passes his Y chromosome to all sons; since the Y does not carry the mutation, the sons will not be affected.
