category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: RFLP Tracking in Autosomal Recessive Pedigrees
statement: A couple has a child with Phenylketonuria (PKU). During a second pregnancy, RFLP analysis shows the fetus has inherited the same 'marker' fragments as the affected sibling from both parents. What is the risk the fetus will manifest PKU?
optionExplanations: 75% is the probability that the child will be phenotypically normal (carriers + homozygous normal).
50% is the probability of an offspring being a carrier, not necessarily affected, unless one parent is affected.
25% is the general probability for any offspring of carrier parents to be affected, but the RFLP results here specifically identify the genotype.

Since the fetus inherited the specific RFLP markers linked to the mutant alleles from both carrier parents (matching the affected sibling), the fetus is homozygous for the mutation and has a 100% chance of having the disease.
A 0% risk would only occur if the fetus inherited normal alleles from both parents.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": In Figure 34.19, examination of fetal DNA shows that the fetus (subject II-4) inherited two abnormal genes from the parents and, therefore, has PKU.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 12-year-old male presents with myoclonic epilepsy and 'ragged red fibers' on skeletal muscle biopsy. His mother and maternal aunt also suffer from milder muscle weakness and seizures, but his father and paternal siblings are unaffected. What is the most probable inheritance pattern?
options: X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial inheritance
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
correctOption: Mitochondrial inheritance
optionExplanations: X-linked dominant inheritance would involve an affected father passing the trait to all his daughters, which is inconsistent with the maternal-only pattern described.
The clinical presentation (MERRF) and the pedigree (maternal transmission only) are classic for mitochondrial inheritance. Mitochondria are inherited only from the mother.
Autosomal recessive traits would likely show affected siblings with phenotypically normal parents, and would not be restricted to the maternal lineage.

X-linked recessive traits usually affect males while females are asymptomatic carriers; however, in this case, the mother and aunt are also symptomatic, and mitochondrial transmission is more specific for this muscle pathology.
Autosomal dominant traits would be seen in both paternal and maternal lines; the strict maternal transmission here argues against autosomes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Mutations in the mitochondrial gene for tRNA Lys are associated with myoclonic epilepsy (jerking muscle spasms) with ragged red fibers (MERRF), a disorder that affects skeletal muscle structure and function.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the context of X-linked recessive disorders such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), which physiological mechanism explains why the clinical phenotype is typically restricted to males in a standard carrier-pedigree?
options: Males are hemizygous, having only one X chromosome derived from the mother
Females undergo selective inactivation of the paternal X chromosome only
Females require two copies of the Y chromosome to express the trait
Males are homozygous for the mutant allele on the autosomes
The mutant gene is located on the Y chromosome in affected individuals
correctOption: Males are hemizygous, having only one X chromosome derived from the mother
optionExplanations: Because males have only one X chromosome (hemizygosity), a single recessive mutation on that chromosome is sufficient to cause the disease phenotype.
X-inactivation (Lyonization) is usually random in females, not restricted to the paternal chromosome, allowing carriers to remain largely asymptomatic.
Females do not typically possess a Y chromosome; they are XX, and X-linked recessive traits require two mutant X alleles for expression in females.
DMD is not an autosomal disorder; it is linked to the X chromosome, so autosomal homozygosity is irrelevant to its primary inheritance.
The DMD gene is located on the X chromosome, not the Y chromosome; Y-linked traits are extremely rare and show male-to-male transmission.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which specific genetic term is defined as the state of having only one copy of a gene or chromosome instead of the usual two, as seen in human males for genes on the X chromosome?
options: Aneuploid
Heterozygous
Homozygous
Codominant
Hemizygous
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Aneuploid refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., 45 or 47 instead of 46).
Heterozygous means having two different alleles at a specific locus.
Homozygous means having two identical alleles at a specific locus.
Codominant refers to a state where both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed (e.g., AB blood group).
Hemizygous is the correct term for having only one allele at a locus, specifically characterizing males (XY) for X-linked genes.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A researcher is studying Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH). If the condition is caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene and follows an autosomal dominant pattern, what is the most likely observation in a large pedigree?
options: Males are affected significantly more frequently than females.
Every affected individual has at least one affected parent.
The trait often skips generations, appearing only when two carriers mate.
Affected fathers pass the trait only to their daughters.
The trait is only expressed if the individual inherits two copies of the mutant gene.
correctOption: Every affected individual has at least one affected parent.
optionExplanations: Equal frequency of affected males and females is characteristic of autosomal inheritance; more frequent males suggest X-linked recessive inheritance.
In autosomal dominant inheritance, the trait is transmitted vertically; thus, every affected person must have at least one parent with the trait, unless it is a de novo mutation.
Skipping generations is a hallmark of autosomal recessive inheritance, not autosomal dominant traits like FH.
Fathers passing only to daughters is characteristic of X-linked dominant inheritance; autosomal traits are passed to both sexes equally.
Inheriting two copies for expression defines a recessive trait. In dominant traits like FH, a single mutant allele is sufficient to produce the phenotype (heterozygotes are affected).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia can also be caused by defects in apo B-100 that reduce its binding to the receptor

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: When analyzing the pedigrees of two separate patients—one with Vitamin D-resistant Rickets and another with Xeroderma Pigmentosum—which diagnostic contrast in their inheritance patterns is most accurate?
options: Rickets is autosomal recessive and requires two carrier parents, whereas Xeroderma Pigmentosum is X-linked dominant.
Rickets is X-linked recessive and affects only males, whereas Xeroderma Pigmentosum is autosomal dominant and shows vertical inheritance.
Rickets is X-linked dominant and affects both sexes, whereas Xeroderma Pigmentosum is autosomal recessive and often involves consanguinity.
Rickets is mitochondrial and passed only by mothers, whereas Xeroderma Pigmentosum is X-linked dominant.
Rickets is autosomal dominant and shows a 50% recurrence risk, whereas Xeroderma Pigmentosum is X-linked recessive.
correctOption: Rickets is X-linked dominant and affects both sexes, whereas Xeroderma Pigmentosum is autosomal recessive and often involves consanguinity.
optionExplanations: Rickets is X-linked dominant. XP is autosomal recessive.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is the X-linked recessive example; Huntington's is the autosomal dominant example.

According to the syllabus, Rickets (specifically the hereditary type mentioned) is X-linked dominant, meaning both males and females can be affected, and an affected male will pass the trait to all his daughters. Xeroderma Pigmentosum is autosomal recessive, meaning it typically appears in siblings of a single generation and is more likely in consanguineous marriages.
Mitochondrial diabetes is the mitochondrial example, not Rickets. XP is not X-linked dominant.
Huntington's is the AD example. Duchenne is X-linked recessive.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: If a female is a carrier of an autosomal recessive mutation for Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) and her partner is homozygous for the wild-type allele, what is the risk of their children being clinically affected by the disorder?
optionExplanations: A 50% risk occurs when one parent is a carrier (Aa) and the other is affected (aa).
A 100% risk occurs when both parents are clinically affected by the same autosomal recessive disorder (aa x aa).
A 25% risk occurs when both parents are carriers (Aa x Aa).
In an autosomal recessive cross (Aa x AA), 50% of children will be carriers (Aa) and 50% will be homozygous normal (AA). None will be homozygous recessive (aa), so the disease risk is 0%.
There is no common Mendelian cross for two unaffected parents that results in a 75% risk.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with progressive involuntary choreiform movements, psychiatric disturbances, and cognitive decline. His father died in his early 50s following a similar clinical course. Molecular analysis confirms a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene. If this patient's son inherits the expanded allele and shows symptoms at age 30, which genetic principle is best demonstrated?
options: Incomplete penetrance
Variable expressivity
Anticipation
Mosaicism
Codominance
correctOption: Anticipation
optionExplanations: Incomplete penetrance occurs when some individuals with the mutation do not develop any symptoms of the disorder at all.
Variable expressivity refers to the range of signs and symptoms that can occur in different people with the same genetic condition, not the timing of onset.
Anticipation is the phenomenon where a genetic disorder (like Huntington's) becomes more severe or has an earlier age of onset in successive generations due to expansion of triplet repeats.
Mosaicism refers to the presence of two or more populations of cells with different genotypes in one individual, usually due to a post-zygotic mutation.
Codominance occurs when both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed, such as in the AB blood group, which is not the case here.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": expansion of the CAG codon in exon 1 of the gene for huntingtin protein leads to the insertion of many extra glutamine residues... causing the neurodegenerative disorder Huntington disease

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Mitochondrial inheritance patterns differ significantly from Mendelian nuclear inheritance. Which structural feature of the mitochondrial genome is characteristic of these traits?
options: Mitochondrial traits follow the law of independent assortment with nuclear genes.
Mitochondria contain closed, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules.
Replication of mitochondrial DNA is strictly synchronized with the S phase of the cell cycle.
The mitochondrial genome consists of a single, large linear chromosome.
Mitochondrial DNA is organized into nucleosomes with histone H1 stabilizers.
correctOption: Mitochondria contain closed, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules.
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial inheritance is non-Mendelian (maternal) and does not follow the law of independent assortment relative to nuclear chromosomes.
Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is unique in eukaryotes for being circular and double-stranded, similar to prokaryotic plasmids, which supports the endosymbiotic theory.
Mitochondrial DNA replication is not strictly synchronized with the nuclear cell cycle and can occur independently of the S phase.
The mitochondrial genome is circular, not linear; nuclear chromosomes are linear.
Mitochondrial DNA is not associated with histones; histones are characteristic of nuclear DNA organization.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Eukaryotes have closed, circular, dsDNA molecules in their mitochondria, as do plant chloroplasts.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the context of Mendelian genetics, which term describes the state of having only one copy of a specific gene in an otherwise diploid cell, as typically seen in human males for genes located on the X chromosome?
options: Hemizygous
Homozygous
Heterozygous
Haploid
Aneuploid
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Hemizygous is the specific term used when only one copy of a gene is present, such as X-linked genes in males (XY) or in the case of a chromosomal deletion.
Homozygous refers to having two identical alleles for a particular gene on homologous chromosomes.
Heterozygous refers to having two different alleles for a particular gene on homologous chromosomes.
Haploid describes a cell having a single set of chromosomes (like gametes), whereas human males are diploid organisms who are hemizygous for the X chromosome.
Aneuploid refers to having an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy), not the state of specific alleles.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which characteristic specifically distinguishes X-linked dominant inheritance from autosomal dominant inheritance in a pedigree?
options: Affected mothers pass the trait to all of their sons but none of their daughters.
Males and females are affected with equal frequency.
The trait often skips a generation through asymptomatic carriers.
Affected fathers pass the trait to all of their daughters but none of their sons.
Affected individuals must have at least one affected parent.
correctOption: Affected fathers pass the trait to all of their daughters but none of their sons.
optionExplanations: An affected mother (heterozygous) in an X-linked dominant pattern has a 50% chance of passing the trait to any child, regardless of the child's gender.
Autosomal dominant traits affect both sexes equally, but X-linked dominant traits typically affect females twice as often as males.
Skipping generations is characteristic of recessive traits, not dominant traits (unless there is significantly reduced penetrance).

In X-linked dominant inheritance, a father provides his only X chromosome (carrying the dominant mutation) to all of his daughters and his Y chromosome to all of his sons. Thus, all daughters are affected and no sons are affected.
This is a feature of both autosomal dominant and X-linked dominant inheritance and therefore does not distinguish between them.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: ... X-linked dominant (Rickets)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A pedigree analysis of a family with a history of a specific neurological disorder shows that the trait appears in every generation. Affected individuals always have at least one affected parent, and the trait is passed to both sons and daughters with equal frequency. Which inheritance pattern most likely explains this observation?
options: Autosomal dominant
Mitochondrial
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
correctOption: Autosomal dominant
optionExplanations: Autosomal dominant traits are characterized by vertical transmission, where the phenotype appears in every generation and each affected person has an affected parent.
Mitochondrial inheritance is characterized by transmission only through females to all of their children; an affected male cannot pass the trait to any offspring.
Autosomal recessive traits typically skip generations and often appear among siblings rather than in a vertical line of descent.
X-linked recessive traits primarily affect males and typically skip generations through carrier females, rather than appearing in every generation for both sexes.

statement: A newborn presents with ambiguous genitalia and is diagnosed with Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) due to a 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Both parents are clinically normal. What does this suggest about the inheritance and metabolic regulation of this condition?
options: It is a mitochondrial trait resulting in oxidative failure
It is an autosomal recessive trait resulting in enzyme deficiency
It is a holandric trait passed only from fathers to sons
It is an X-linked dominant trait affecting steroid receptors
It is an autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation
correctOption: It is an autosomal recessive trait resulting in enzyme deficiency
optionExplanations: While some mitochondrial enzymes are involved in steroidogenesis, CAH is classified as a nuclear autosomal recessive trait.
CAH is a group of autosomal recessive disorders where both alleles must be defective, leading to a specific enzyme deficiency (like 21-hydroxylase) in the adrenal cortex.
Holandric traits are Y-linked; CAH affects both males and females equally, confirming its autosomal nature.
CAH affects enzyme levels, not the steroid receptors, and it is not X-linked dominant.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: X-linked Recessive Risk Assessment in Pedigrees
statement: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for progressive gait abnormality and difficulty rising from a seated position. Physical examination reveals pseudohypertrophy of the calves and a positive Gowers' sign. His maternal uncle died of a similar muscle-wasting disease at age 18. Genetic analysis of the boy's dystrophin gene reveals a significant deletion. If the boy's mother is pregnant with a male fetus, what is the calculated risk that the fetus will be affected by the same condition?
options: 75% risk, because X-linked recessive traits show high recurrence in males.
25% risk, because both parents must be carriers for the trait to manifest.
50% risk, assuming the mother is a heterozygous carrier of the X-linked mutation.
100% risk, as all male offspring of a carrier mother are affected.
0% risk, as the father is unaffected and the trait is not autosomal.
correctOption: 50% risk, assuming the mother is a heterozygous carrier of the X-linked mutation.
optionExplanations: 75% is not a standard Mendelian ratio for a single-gene X-linked recessive cross between a carrier female and a normal male.
A 25% risk (1 in 4 total children) is the risk for autosomal recessive conditions, but for a known male fetus in an X-linked recessive scenario, the risk is specifically 50%.

Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is X-linked recessive. Since the boy is affected and there is a positive maternal family history, the mother is a carrier. She has a 50% chance of passing the mutant X to any male fetus, making him affected.
Not all sons are affected; there is a 50% chance the son will inherit the normal X chromosome from the mother.
While the father is unaffected, the boy's condition and family history (maternal uncle) strongly indicate the mother is an X-linked carrier, posing a risk to male offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: During the replication of human genetic material, the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) is distinct because it is essentially a closed, circular dsDNA molecule. Which statement regarding the inheritance of these specific genetic units is biologically accurate?
options: The mitochondrial genome is only present in males.
Mitochondrial inheritance follows the Mendelian Law of Independent Assortment.
Mitochondrial DNA is exclusively of maternal origin.
Sperm cells contribute the majority of the mitochondrial population to the zygote.
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from both parents via the nuclear scaffold.
correctOption: Mitochondrial DNA is exclusively of maternal origin.
optionExplanations: Mitochondria are essential for energy metabolism in all human cells, regardless of the sex of the individual.
Mendelian laws apply to nuclear genes on chromosomes, not to the cytoplasmic inheritance of mitochondrial DNA.

In humans, mitochondrial inheritance is exclusively maternal. The oocyte provides the vast majority of the cytoplasm and mitochondria to the zygote, while paternal mitochondria are typically degraded.
Sperm cells contribute very few, if any, mitochondria to the zygote; the oocyte is the primary source.
MtDNA is not inherited through the nuclear scaffold and is not biparental; it is extra-chromosomal and uniparental.

statement: Which term best describes the genetic status of a male with a single mutant allele on the X-chromosome for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD)?
options: Aneuploid
Homozygous
Hemizygous
Codominant
Heterozygous
correctOption: Hemizygous
optionExplanations: Aneuploid refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy), which is not the standard descriptor for a single gene mutation on a normal sex chromosome.
Homozygous implies having two identical alleles; again, males only have one X chromosome.
Hemizygous is the term used to describe the genotype of an individual who has only one representative of a chromosome or chromosome segment, specifically males for genes on the X and Y chromosomes.
Codominant refers to a relationship between two alleles where both are expressed; this is not possible for a single allele in a hemizygous male.
Heterozygous implies having two different alleles at a locus; males have only one X chromosome and thus cannot be heterozygous for X-linked genes.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: When comparing the transmission of X-linked recessive traits to X-linked dominant traits, which diagnostic contrast is observed regarding the offspring of an affected father?
options: In X-linked recessive, all daughters are carriers; in X-linked dominant, all daughters are affected.
In X-linked recessive, no daughters receive the allele; in X-linked dominant, all sons receive the allele.
In X-linked recessive, all daughters are affected; in X-linked dominant, all daughters are carriers.
In X-linked recessive, 50% of sons are affected; in X-linked dominant, 100% of sons are affected.
In X-linked recessive, all sons are carriers; in X-linked dominant, all daughters are carriers.
correctOption: In X-linked recessive, all daughters are carriers; in X-linked dominant, all daughters are affected.
optionExplanations: Correct. Since a father must give his X chromosome to all daughters, an affected father with an X-linked dominant trait will have 100% affected daughters. If the trait is X-linked recessive, the daughters will all be obligate carriers.
Incorrect. All daughters receive the X chromosome from their father, regardless of the dominance pattern. Sons receive the Y chromosome.
Incorrect. It is the reverse; X-linked dominant fathers pass the trait (affected) to all daughters, while X-linked recessive fathers pass the allele (carrier status) to all daughters.
Incorrect. Fathers do not pass X chromosomes to their sons; therefore, an affected father cannot pass an X-linked trait to his son.
Incorrect. Sons are hemizygous; they cannot be 'carriers' of X-linked traits. They either have the allele (and the disease) or they don't.

statement: In a clinical genetics setting, which characteristic is uniquely indicative of an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern when analyzing a multi-generational pedigree?
options: The trait often skips generations, appearing only in the offspring of unaffected carriers.
Affected individuals must have at least one affected parent in every generation without skipping.
Affected fathers pass the trait to all of their daughters but none of their sons.
The trait is expressed primarily in males, with females acting as unaffected carriers.
The trait is transmitted exclusively through the maternal line to all offspring.
correctOption: Affected individuals must have at least one affected parent in every generation without skipping.
optionExplanations: Skipping generations is a hallmark of autosomal recessive traits, where carriers do not manifest the phenotype.
Autosomal dominant traits typically do not skip generations; an affected child must have an affected parent because the presence of a single mutant allele is sufficient for phenotypic expression.
This is characteristic of X-linked dominant inheritance, where a father's single X chromosome is passed to all daughters and his Y to all sons.
This describes X-linked recessive inheritance, where males are hemizygous and females are protected by a second X chromosome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits

statement: In a pedigree analysis of a large kindred, a specific trait is found to affect both males and females. X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial
Autosomal dominant
Y-linked
correctOption: Autosomal dominant
optionExplanations: Recessive traits usually skip generations and often appear in the offspring of unaffected (carrier) parents.
X-linked recessive traits predominantly affect males and typically skip generations through carrier females.
Mitochondrial inheritance would result in none of the affected father's children being affected, as mitochondria are inherited only from the mother.

Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation (vertical transmission) and affect both sexes. An affected heterozygous parent has a 50% chance of passing the trait to any child, consistent with having 2 affected and 2 unaffected children.
Y-linked traits only affect males and would be passed from an affected father to all of his sons and none of his daughters.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: RFLP and Linkage in Autosomal Recessive Disorders
statement: In the context of the indirect diagnosis of an autosomal recessive condition like Phenylketonuria (PKU), why must the DNA of the parents and an affected sibling be analyzed to determine the fetal status using Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphisms (RFLP)?
options: To ensure the fetus has inherited the mitochondrial DNA from the mother.
To count the number of CAG triplet repeats in the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene.
To confirm that the gene has undergone somatic rearrangement in the liver cells.
To determine which specific RFLP pattern is linked to the mutant allele in that specific family.
To verify that the father is hemizygous for the phenylalanine hydroxylase mutation.
correctOption: To determine which specific RFLP pattern is linked to the mutant allele in that specific family.
optionExplanations: PKU is an autosomal recessive nuclear DNA disorder, not a mitochondrial DNA disorder.
CAG repeats are characteristic of Huntington's disease (autosomal dominant), not PKU. PKU is typically caused by point mutations, deletions, or insertions in the PAH gene.
Somatic rearrangement occurs in immunoglobulin genes in B lymphocytes, not in the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene in hepatocytes or fetal cells.

Because many different mutations can cause PKU, indirect diagnosis uses RFLPs as markers. Since RFLPs are just variations in DNA sequence, we must look at an affected family member to see which marker (e.g., fragment 'a' or 'b') travels with the mutant allele in that particular family.
PKU is autosomal; therefore, individuals have two copies of the gene. 'Hemizygous' refers to having only one copy (like X-linked genes in males), which is incorrect for PKU.

statement: A 4-year-old male presents with difficulty rising from a seated position and pseudohypertrophy of the calves. Genetic testing confirms a deletion in the dystrophin gene. The mother is clinically normal, but her brother died of a similar condition in his teens. What is the most accurate assessment of the inheritance risk for this family?
options: The disorder is mitochondrial, inherited solely through the maternal cytoplasm.
The father must be a carrier of the mutated gene to have an affected son.
The disorder is autosomal dominant, and the mother is a mosaic for the mutation.
All future daughters of this mother have a 50% risk of manifesting severe symptoms.
There is a 50% probability that any future son of this mother will be affected.
correctOption: There is a 50% probability that any future son of this mother will be affected.
optionExplanations: DMD is a nuclear gene mutation (dystrophin gene), not a mitochondrial DNA mutation.
In X-linked recessive inheritance, the father does not need to be a carrier; he provides the Y chromosome to the son.
DMD is X-linked recessive, not autosomal dominant.
In X-linked recessive disorders like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), daughters of a carrier mother have a 50% chance of being carriers but are typically asymptomatic.
Correct. A carrier mother (XbX) has a 50% chance of passing the mutant X chromosome (Xb) to her sons, who will then be hemizygous and affected.

Codominant

Homozygous refers to having two identical alleles at a locus, impossible for X-linked genes in normal XY males.
Heterozygous refers to having two different alleles at a locus, which requires two copies of the chromosome (e.g., in females).
Aneuploid refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., 47 instead of 46), not the state of alleles on a single chromosome.

The trait is only expressed in males (hemizygous).
Affected males transmit the condition to all of their daughters.

Affected females transmit the condition to all of their offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the study of Mendelian genetics, which feature is uniquely characteristic of an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern in a typical multi-generational pedigree?
options: The trait is expressed only when the individual is homozygous for the mutant allele.
Affected individuals must have at least one affected parent to manifest the phenotype.
Females are twice as likely to be affected as males due to dosage compensation.
The trait typically skips generations, appearing only in the offspring of unaffected carriers.
Male-to-male transmission of the trait is impossible due to the chromosomal location.
correctOption: Affected individuals must have at least one affected parent to manifest the phenotype.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes a recessive trait, which requires two copies of the mutant allele to be phenotypically visible.
Correct. In autosomal dominant traits, an affected person usually has an affected parent (vertical transmission), as the presence of a single mutant allele is sufficient for expression.
Incorrect. This is not characteristic of autosomal dominant traits; both sexes are generally affected with equal frequency.
Incorrect. Skipping generations (horizontal transmission) is a hallmark of autosomal recessive inheritance, where carriers do not show the phenotype.
Incorrect. Male-to-male transmission occurs in autosomal traits because the genes are located on non-sex chromosomes.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: Molecular Basis of Autosomal Recessive Traits (Sickle Cell)
statement: Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disease. What specific type of mutation at the DNA level is responsible for the creation of the HbS allele?
options: A frameshift mutation in the first exon.
A triplet repeat expansion in the 3' untranslated region.
A point mutation causing a single nucleotide change.
A large deletion of the promoter region.
An insertion of a transposon into the coding sequence.
correctOption: A point mutation causing a single nucleotide change.
optionExplanations: Frameshift mutations usually result in truncated or radically different proteins; HbS is the result of a single amino acid substitution.
Triplet repeat expansions are characteristic of diseases like Huntington's, not sickle cell anemia.
Sickle cell anemia is the classic example of a point mutation where a single base change (A to T) leads to a different amino acid (Glutamate to Valine).
Promoter deletions would lead to a lack of protein production (thalassemia), not the production of an abnormal hemoglobin variant like HbS.
Transposon insertions are rare causes of disease and typically disrupt the gene entirely rather than creating a specific functional variant like HbS.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the UHS pediatrics department with severe bowing of the legs and growth retardation. Laboratory tests show low serum phosphate and resistance to Vitamin D treatment. The family pedigree reveals that the patient's father is affected, but her mother is normal. All of the patient's sisters are affected, while her only brother is completely normal. What is the most likely mode of inheritance?
options: Mitochondrial
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
correctOption: X-linked dominant
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial inheritance would require the mother to be affected to pass it to the children.
In X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected father cannot have affected daughters unless the mother is at least a carrier.
In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected father passes his only (affected) X chromosome to all daughters, making them all affected, and his Y to all sons, making them all normal.
Autosomal dominant would likely result in approximately 50% of both sons and daughters being affected, not a gender-specific split (all daughters, no sons).
In autosomal recessive inheritance, an affected father and normal mother would likely have normal (carrier) children.

Heterozygous

Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy), not the state of alleles on a single chromosome.

statement: A woman is diagnosed with Myoclonic Epilepsy and Ragged Red Fibers (MERRF) due to a mutation in a mitochondrial tRNA gene. She is concerned about passing this trait to her offspring. According to the principles of non-Mendelian inheritance associated with this organelle, what should she be told?

Only her daughters will develop the disease, while her sons will be unaffected.
All of her children will likely inherit the mutation, though the severity may vary.
The trait will only manifest if her partner also carries the same mitochondrial mutation.
There is no risk to her children because mitochondrial DNA is only inherited from the father.
correctOption: All of her children will likely inherit the mutation, though the severity may vary.
optionExplanations: MERRF does not follow autosomal recessive Mendelian ratios because the genes are located on the mitochondrial circular DNA, not on nuclear chromosomes.
Mitochondrial DNA is passed to all children of an affected mother, not just daughters, as both receive their cytoplasm and organelles from the egg.

statement: The neurodegenerative disorder Huntington disease is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene. Based on the biochemical mechanism where the presence of the expanded CAG sequence leads to toxic protein fragments, what is the characteristic inheritance pattern?
options: Autosomal dominant
Holandric
Mitochondrial
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive

optionExplanations: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder. The expansion of CAG repeats creates a toxic protein product that causes disease even in the presence of a normal allele (heterozygosity).
Holandric (Y-linked) traits are only passed from fathers to sons; Huntington's affects daughters as well.
The disease is encoded by nuclear DNA, not mitochondrial DNA, and can be transmitted by either parent.

Autosomal recessive disorders usually involve a loss of enzyme activity that can be compensated for by a single normal allele; Huntington's involves a toxic gain of function from a single mutant allele.
Huntington's is not located on the X chromosome and affects both males and females, which is inconsistent with X-linked recessive patterns.

statement: A specific enzyme deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. If two asymptomatic individuals who are both known carriers for this mutation have children, what is the underlying genetic probability regarding the offspring's genotype?
options: Each child has a 50% probability of being a symptomatic homozygote.
There is a 25% probability that each child will be a homozygous normal individual.
Each child has a 75% probability of being a symptomatic homozygote.
All children will inevitably be carriers due to the parental carrier status.
100% of the daughters will be carriers while 100% of the sons will be normal.
correctOption: There is a 25% probability that each child will be a homozygous normal individual.
optionExplanations: A 50% probability of being affected would only occur if one parent was affected (aa) and the other was a carrier (Aa).
Correct. When both parents are carriers (Aa x Aa), there is a 25% (1/4) chance of the child inheriting the normal allele from both parents (AA).
In autosomal recessive inheritance, the probability of being a symptomatic homozygote (inheriting two mutant alleles) is 25%, not 75%.
The probability of being a carrier (Aa) is 50%, not 100%, as there is a 25% chance of being homozygous normal and 25% chance of being homozygous mutant.
This describes a sex-influenced or X-linked pattern; autosomal recessive traits affect both sexes with equal probability.

X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant

optionExplanations: Autosomal dominant traits would be passed to 50% of sons and 50% of daughters from an affected father; they do not show the sex-dependent transmission seen here.
In X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected father cannot pass the trait to his sons, but his daughters would only be carriers (unaffected) unless the mother also provided a mutant allele.
Mitochondrial inheritance involves transmission only from the mother; an affected father would have zero affected children.

statement: Which of the following best describes a key feature of mitochondrial inheritance that differentiates it from nuclear genetic patterns?
options: Genes are located on linear chromosomes within the nucleus
The genome consists of closed, circular, double-stranded DNA
It involves the random segregation of alleles during meiosis
Traits are only expressed in males due to hemizygosity
It follows a strict 3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation

optionExplanations: Mitochondrial genes are extranuclear and located on circular DNA, not on the linear chromosomes found in the nucleus.
Unlike nuclear DNA, mitochondrial DNA is a small, circular, double-stranded molecule that is replicated independently.
Mitochondrial inheritance does not involve Mendelian segregation or meiosis-driven independent assortment of nuclear alleles.
Mitochondrial traits affect both males and females; hemizygosity is a term describing X-linked genes in males.
The 3:1 ratio is a Mendelian principle for autosomal recessive traits in the F2 generation, which does not apply to mitochondrial DNA.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A patient is identified as having Familial Hypercholesterolemia (Type IIa), an autosomal dominant condition. If the patient is heterozygous for a loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene, what is the expected physiological impact on their LDL receptor density and plasma cholesterol compared to a normal individual?
options: Increase in receptor density; decrease in plasma LDL-C due to gain-of-function.
50% reduction in functional receptor density; significant elevation in plasma LDL-C.
100% receptor density; normal plasma cholesterol due to compensatory upregulation.
0% receptor density; normal plasma cholesterol because the other allele becomes hyperactive.
Normal receptor density; elevation of cholesterol only if the diet is high in fat.
correctOption: 50% reduction in functional receptor density; significant elevation in plasma LDL-C.
optionExplanations: This would describe a PCSK9 gain-of-function or a beneficial mutation, not the standard loss-of-function seen in typical FH.
Heterozygous FH is characterized by a roughly 50% reduction in functional LDL receptors. This 'dosage' effect leads to impaired clearance of LDL from the plasma and premature atherosclerosis.
In an AD loss-of-function condition, one mutant allele is enough to cause disease because 50% of the gene product is insufficient for normal function.
0% receptor density is seen in homozygous FH, which is a much more severe clinical presentation.
In FH, the cholesterol elevation is primary and genetic, persisting regardless of a low-fat diet, though diet can influence the magnitude of the levels.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Defects in the synthesis of functional LDL receptors causes a significant elevation in plasma LDL- C. Patients with such deficiencies have type IIa hyperlipidemia [familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)]

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (SLOS) is a multisystem embryonic malformation syndrome. Given that it is caused by a partial deficiency in 7-dehydrocholesterol-7-reductase, what is its characteristic inheritance pattern?
options: X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial
X-linked dominant
Autosomal recessive
Autosomal dominant
correctOption: Autosomal recessive
optionExplanations: X-linked recessive inheritance is less common for general metabolic enzymes of cholesterol synthesis, which are typically encoded on autosomes.
Mitochondrial inheritance involves mitochondrial DNA; SLOS is caused by a mutation in a nuclear gene encoding an enzyme of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER).
X-linked dominant patterns are rare for metabolic enzyme pathways and do not match the clinical description of SLOS.
Enzyme deficiencies, such as the one in SLOS, typically follow an autosomal recessive pattern because a single functional allele usually produces enough enzyme to maintain health.
Autosomal dominant conditions usually result from structural protein defects or gain-of-function mutations, rather than simple enzyme deficiencies.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome (SLOS), an autosomal-recessive disorder of cholesterol biosynthesis, is caused by a partial deficiency in 7- dehydrocholesterol-7-reductase.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In a pedigree analysis for a family with Vitamin D-resistant Rickets, it is observed that an affected male has four daughters, all of whom are affected, and three sons, none of whom are affected. Which mode of inheritance is most consistent with this pattern?
options: X-linked Recessive
X-linked Dominant
Autosomal Dominant
Autosomal Recessive
Mitochondrial
correctOption: X-linked Dominant
optionExplanations: In X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected father would pass the gene to his daughters making them carriers, not necessarily affected, and his sons would be unaffected.

In X-linked dominant inheritance, an affected male passes his single affected X chromosome to all of his daughters (making them affected) and his Y chromosome to all of his sons (leaving them unaffected).
In autosomal dominant inheritance, an affected father would have a 50% chance of passing the trait to both sons and daughters, not 100% of daughters and 0% of sons.
Autosomal recessive traits typically skip generations and would not show this gender-specific transmission pattern from an affected father.
Mitochondrial traits are never passed from a father to his children, as mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the maternal line.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: ... 2) X-linked dominant (Rickets)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A healthy woman whose brother has Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is found to be a carrier of the dystrophin gene mutation. If she has a son, what is the biochemical and genetic likelihood of him being affected by the disease?
options: He has a 50% chance of being a carrier but will not express the disease.
He has a 100% chance of being affected because his mother is a carrier.
He has a 0% chance of being affected because his father is healthy.
He has a 50% chance of being affected because he will inherit only one X chromosome.
He has a 25% chance of being affected, as the disease is autosomal recessive.
correctOption: He has a 50% chance of being affected because he will inherit only one X chromosome.
optionExplanations: Males cannot be 'carriers' of X-linked recessive traits; they are either hemizygous normal or hemizygous affected.
The risk is not 100% because the mother has two X chromosomes; the son has a 50% chance of inheriting the normal X chromosome.
The father's health does not prevent the son from being affected in X-linked recessive traits because the son inherits his X chromosome exclusively from his mother.

Males are hemizygous for the X chromosome. A son of a carrier mother has a 50% chance of inheriting the X chromosome with the mutant dystrophin allele. If he inherits it, he will be affected because he has no second X chromosome to mask the mutation.
DMD is X-linked recessive, not autosomal recessive. The 25% figure would only apply to the overall risk for any child (male or female) if we didn't specify the sex of the son.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Regarding the inheritance of mitochondrial traits, how many genes are found on the human mitochondrial chromosome and what is the characteristic of their transmission?
options: 22 tRNA genes, transmitted exclusively by the mother to all offspring.
5S rRNA genes, transmitted only to daughters.
13 genes, transmitted exclusively by the father.
22 genes, transmitted exclusively by the mother.
46 genes, transmitted to 50% of offspring by either parent.
correctOption: 22 tRNA genes, transmitted exclusively by the mother to all offspring.
optionExplanations: The mitochondrial genome includes 22 tRNA genes and is characterized by maternal inheritance, where an affected mother passes the trait to all her children.
5S rRNA is encoded by nuclear DNA (RNA polymerase III), not mitochondrial DNA, and mitochondrial traits affect both genders.
Mitochondrial DNA is not transmitted by the father; paternal mitochondria are typically excluded from the zygote.
While the chromosome does have 22 tRNA genes, the total gene count is higher (including protein-coding genes), but the transmission is maternal.
The human mitochondrial chromosome does not contain 46 genes, and it does not follow a 50% random Mendelian segregation like autosomes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": The human mitochondrial chromosome carries 22 tRNA genes... mutations in these genes can cause human disease... [Mitochondrial traits] Mitochondrial diabetes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A patient with high plasma cholesterol is found to have a defect in the LDL receptor gene that prevents the recycling of the receptor to the cell surface. The patient's mother and several siblings also have severely elevated cholesterol levels and premature atherosclerosis. This condition, Familial Hypercholesterolemia (Type IIa), is most commonly inherited as which type of trait?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial
X-linked recessive
correctOption: Autosomal dominant
optionExplanations: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) is a classic example of an autosomal dominant disorder, where a single mutated allele for the LDL receptor (or apo B-100) is sufficient to cause significantly elevated cholesterol.
While some rare forms of hyperlipidemia are recessive, the standard FH (Type IIa) described is autosomal dominant.
X-linked dominant inheritance is less common and would show a specific pattern of all-daughter transmission from affected fathers, which is not the case for FH.
Mitochondrial inheritance would exclude transmission from an affected father, but FH can be inherited from either parent.
X-linked recessive traits do not show the equal distribution among male and female family members seen in FH pedigrees.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Patients with such deficiencies have type IIa hyperlipidemia [familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)] and premature atherosclerosis... Autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia can also be caused by defects in apo B-100

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder. At the molecular level, what is the most common consequence of the ΔF508 mutation on the CFTR protein product?
options: Inability to bind the signal recognition particle for RER targeting.
Incorrect folding leading to proteasomal degradation of the protein.
Conversion of the mRNA from monocistronic to polycistronic.
Increased protein stability resulting in accumulation in the Golgi.
Creation of a cryptic splice site leading to intron retention.
correctOption: Incorrect folding leading to proteasomal degradation of the protein.
optionExplanations: The protein is still targeted to the RER, but it fails the folding quality check within the RER and is subsequently degraded.
The loss of phenylalanine at position 508 causes the protein to misfold. The cell's quality control mechanism marks it with ubiquitin for degradation by the proteasome.
Eukaryotic mRNAs are inherently monocistronic; mutations in coding regions do not change this fundamental structural property of the transcript.
The mutation decreases stability; correctly folded CFTR is required for transport to the plasma membrane, not the Golgi.
While splice site mutations occur in CF, the ΔF508 is a specific 3-base deletion in the coding region, not a splice site mutation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": This ΔF508 mutation prevents normal folding of CFTR, leading to its destruction by the proteasome

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: When distinguishing between X-linked recessive and autosomal dominant inheritance in a multi-generational pedigree, which biological finding provides absolute evidence against an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance?
options: The disorder appearing in a hemizygous male.
The presence of an affected female whose father is also affected.
Affected males having only unaffected daughters.
A single instance of male-to-male transmission of the trait.
The observation of the trait skipping one generation.
correctOption: A single instance of male-to-male transmission of the trait.
optionExplanations: X-linked recessive traits are classically defined by their appearance in hemizygous males who have only one X chromosome. This supports, rather than disproves, the pattern.
Affected females in X-linked recessive disorders are rare but possible if the father is affected and the mother is a carrier; this does not disprove the pattern.
If the mother is not a carrier, an affected male with an X-linked recessive trait will have only carrier (unaffected) daughters; this is expected.
Male-to-male transmission is impossible for X-linked traits because a father always contributes his Y chromosome to his son. Its presence proves the gene must be on an autosome.
Skipping generations is common in X-linked recessive inheritance as the trait is carried by unaffected females; it is not evidence against the pattern.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Define the following terms: ... hemizygous, autosome

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 5-year-old male is brought to the clinic due to progressive proximal muscle weakness and pseudo-hypertrophy of the calves. Genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. His mother is currently pregnant with a male fetus. Which statement regarding the inheritance and risk in this family is most accurate?
options: Daughters of the affected boy will have a 50% chance of being affected.
The condition follows a mitochondrial inheritance pattern from the maternal line.
There is a 50% chance that the male fetus will be affected by the disorder.
The mother has a 100% probability of being a carrier of the mutation.
The father must be a carrier for the boy to have inherited the condition.
correctOption: There is a 50% chance that the male fetus will be affected by the disorder.
optionExplanations: The affected boy will pass his mutant X to all his daughters, making them carriers (obligate heterozygotes), but they will usually not be affected.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is explicitly X-linked recessive, not mitochondrial, as per the clinical and genetic classification in the curriculum.
DMD is X-linked recessive. If the mother is a carrier (the standard assumption in such pedigree questions), she has a 50% chance of passing the mutant X to any son, making him affected.
While likely if there is a family history, a significant portion of DMD cases result from de novo mutations in the child; the mother is not automatically a 100% certain carrier without testing.
In X-linked recessive inheritance, the father cannot be a 'carrier'; he is either affected (hemizygous) or unaffected. If he were affected, he would pass the trait to his daughters, not his sons.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: 1) X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the context of carbohydrate metabolism regulation, the textbook notes that 'Mitochondrial diabetes' follows a specific inheritance pattern. Which of the following best describes the expected transmission of this disorder from a father who has the condition?
options: He will pass it to 50% of his children, regardless of their sex.
He will pass it to all of his sons but none of his daughters.
He will pass it to all of his children because the trait is dominant.
He will pass it only to his daughters, who will be asymptomatic carriers.
He will not pass the condition to any of his offspring.
correctOption: He will not pass the condition to any of his offspring.
optionExplanations: This describes autosomal inheritance, where either parent can contribute the allele.
This would describe Y-linked inheritance, which is not applicable to mitochondrial DNA.
Mitochondrial inheritance is not 'dominant' in the Mendelian sense, and regardless of its expression, it is not transmitted by males.
This is characteristic of X-linked recessive inheritance, not mitochondrial.

Mitochondrial DNA is inherited exclusively from the mother. An affected father cannot pass his mitochondrial genome (and thus any associated mutations like mitochondrial diabetes) to any of his children.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: ... Mitochondrial disorder (Mitochondrial diabetes)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following inheritance patterns is most likely if a specific trait is observed to affect both males and females in every generation, with each affected child typically having at least one affected parent?
options: X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant
Mitochondrial inheritance
correctOption: Autosomal dominant
optionExplanations: X-linked recessive traits predominantly affect males and frequently show a diagonal transmission pattern (grandfather to grandson via a carrier mother) rather than appearing in every generation.

Autosomal dominant traits are characterized by vertical transmission, appearing in every generation. Both sexes are equally likely to be affected, and affected individuals usually have an affected parent.
Autosomal recessive traits often skip generations and typically appear only in siblings rather than appearing vertically in every generation of a pedigree.

While X-linked dominant traits show vertical transmission, an affected father would transmit the trait to all of his daughters and none of his sons, which is more restrictive than the generalized autosomal pattern described.

Mitochondrial inheritance is characterized by maternal transmission to all children; an affected male does not pass the trait to his offspring, which contradicts the vertical transmission seen in this scenario.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: ... Autosomal dominant (Huntington’s Disease))

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: Mendelian Ratios in Autosomal Recessive Traits
statement: A couple has one child with Phenylketonuria (PKU). While planning for a second pregnancy, they ask about the probability that their next child will be an unaffected carrier. Which of the following is the correct probability?
optionExplanations: 66% (2 in 3) is the probability that an *unaffected* child is a carrier, but for any given pregnancy at the start, the probability is 50%.
In a cross between two carriers (Aa x Aa) for an autosomal recessive trait like PKU, the genotypic ratio is 1AA : 2Aa : 1aa. Thus, there is a 2/4 or 50% probability of having a carrier child.
100% is only possible if one parent is homozygous affected and the other is homozygous normal, which is not the case for two carrier parents.
25% is the probability that the child will be affected (homozygous recessive) or homozygous normal; it is not the probability for being a carrier.
75% is the probability that the child will be phenotypically normal (AA + Aa), not specifically a carrier.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Mutations in the PAH gene usually do not directly affect any restriction endonuclease recognition site. To establish a diagnostic protocol for PKU, DNA from family members of the affected individual must be analyzed. ... subjects II-1 and II-3 were carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In a family pedigree for an X-linked recessive disorder, if an unaffected woman (whose father was affected) marries an unaffected man, what is the predicted outcome for their sons?
options: All sons will be affected.
All sons will be hemizygous normal.
None of the sons will inherit the mutant allele.
50% of the sons are expected to be affected.
All sons will be unaffected carriers.
correctOption: 50% of the sons are expected to be affected.
optionExplanations: Only if the mother were homozygous for the mutation would all sons be affected. In this case, she is a carrier (heterozygous).
While 50% of the sons will be hemizygous normal, the other 50% are expected to inherit the mutant X from the carrier mother.
Since the mother is a carrier, there is a 50% chance each son will inherit the mutant allele and be affected.

The mother is an obligate carrier because her father was affected. She has two X chromosomes (one normal, one mutant). Each son has a 50% chance of receiving the X with the mutation, making him affected.
Males cannot be 'unaffected carriers' for X-linked recessive traits; they are either hemizygous normal or hemizygous affected.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: 1) X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 22-year-old female presents with recurrent seizures, muscle weakness, and exercise intolerance. Laboratory findings reveal significant lactic acidosis. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA Lys gene. What pattern of inheritance is characteristic of this condition?
options: The trait skips generations and affects only males
Transmission follows the Law of Independent Assortment
Females are more severely affected due to X-inactivation
Affected fathers pass the trait to all their sons
Affected mothers pass the trait to all their children
correctOption: Affected mothers pass the trait to all their children
optionExplanations: Skipping generations and male predilection are hallmarks of X-linked recessive inheritance, not mitochondrial traits.
Mitochondrial inheritance is non-Mendelian and does not follow the Law of Independent Assortment, as the genes are not located on nuclear chromosomes.
X-inactivation (Lyonization) is a phenomenon of X-chromosomal genes in females, not mitochondrial DNA.
Mitochondria are inherited almost exclusively from the oocyte; thus, affected fathers do not pass mitochondrial traits to any of their children.
Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is maternally inherited; an affected mother transmits the mutation to all of her children, though clinical severity may vary due to heteroplasmy.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Mutations in the mitochondrial gene for tRNA Lys are associated with myoclonic epilepsy (jerking muscle spasms) with ragged red fibers (MERRF), a disorder that affects skeletal muscle structure and function (myopathy), and with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A patient is diagnosed with Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH), which follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Which molecular mechanism explains why a single mutant allele results in the disease phenotype in this individual?
options: The mutant protein is targeted for mitochondrial degradation, depleting ATP stores.
The mutant allele produces a protein that interferes with the normal protein's function (dominant negative).
The mutation only manifests if the individual is exposed to a high-fat diet (environmental trigger).
A 50% reduction in functional LDL receptors is insufficient to maintain normal cholesterol homeostasis.
The normal allele is epigenetically silenced, leaving only the mutant allele active.
correctOption: A 50% reduction in functional LDL receptors is insufficient to maintain normal cholesterol homeostasis.
optionExplanations: The LDL receptor is a plasma membrane protein, not a mitochondrial protein; FH does not involve mitochondrial ATP depletion.
While some AD traits are dominant negative, FH is primarily a case of haploinsufficiency where one normal allele cannot produce enough receptors.
FH is a genetic disorder; while diet modulates it, the phenotype (elevated LDL) is present regardless of diet due to the receptor defect.
Correct. Autosomal dominant disorders often involve haploinsufficiency, where 50% of the normal gene product (LDL receptors in FH) is not enough for normal physiological function.
Epigenetic silencing (imprinting) is not the standard mechanism for FH inheritance.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Defects in the synthesis of functional LDL receptors causes a significant elevation in plasma LDL- C. Patients with such deficiencies have type IIa hyperlipidemia [familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)]... autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: Which of the following inheritance patterns is most characteristically associated with a 25% risk of recurrence in siblings when both parents are phenotypically normal but are asymptomatic carriers?
options: Mitochondrial inheritance
Y-linked inheritance
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked dominant
correctOption: Autosomal recessive
optionExplanations: Mitochondrial traits are inherited exclusively through the maternal line; an affected male cannot pass the trait to any of his offspring, regardless of the partner's status.
Y-linked inheritance involves genes on the Y chromosome; only males are affected, and an affected father passes the trait to all of his sons.
Autosomal dominant traits usually appear in every generation; a single mutant allele from one parent is sufficient to cause the phenotype, typically resulting in a 50% recurrence risk for offspring.

Autosomal recessive inheritance requires two copies of the mutant gene for the disease to manifest. When both parents are carriers (heterozygotes), there is a 25% chance for each child to be affected.

X-linked dominant traits are passed from an affected father to all of his daughters but none of his sons; they do not typically present with phenotypically normal carrier parents in this specific ratio.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Some of the lysosomal storage diseases result from rare autosomal-recessive deficiencies in the ability to hydrolyze lysosomal cholesteryl esters [Wolman disease] or to transport free cholesterol out of the lysosome [Niemann–Pick disease, type C].

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A mother is a known carrier of an X-linked recessive mutation for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. Her partner is genetically normal. What is the expected phenotype of their offspring?
options: All sons will be affected and all daughters will be carriers.
50% of daughters will be clinically affected due to X-inactivation.
All sons will be healthy because they inherit the normal X from the father.
All children will be healthy but 100% of daughters will be carriers.
50% of sons will be affected and 50% of daughters will be carriers.
correctOption: 50% of sons will be affected and 50% of daughters will be carriers.
optionExplanations: This outcome would only happen if the mother was homozygous affected (very rare in DMD) and the father was normal.
Daughters are typically asymptomatic carriers in XLR inheritance; X-inactivation usually leaves enough functional protein to prevent clinical disease.
Sons inherit the Y chromosome from the father; their X chromosome must come from the mother. If the mother is a carrier, they have a 50% risk of disease.
This describes the cross between an affected father (XhY) and a normal mother (XX).
A carrier mother (XhX) has a 50% chance of passing the Xh to any child. Sons (XhY) will be affected, and daughters (XhX) will be asymptomatic carriers.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Analyze pedigree to determine the mode of inheritance of following traits: 1) X-linked recessive (Duchenne Muscular dystrophy)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In a pedigree exhibiting mitochondrial inheritance for a specific metabolic disorder, what is the expected distribution of the trait among the offspring of an affected female?
options: All children, regardless of sex, will inherit the trait.
Approximately 50% of both sons and daughters will be affected.
Only the daughters will manifest the clinical phenotype.
The trait will skip a generation and appear in the grandsons.
Only the sons will manifest the clinical phenotype.
correctOption: All children, regardless of sex, will inherit the trait.
optionExplanations: Correct. Since mitochondria are inherited almost exclusively from the oocyte, an affected mother will pass the mitochondrial mutation to all of her biological children.
A 50% distribution is characteristic of autosomal dominant or X-linked patterns, not the uniparental maternal transmission of mitochondria.
Mitochondrial DNA is not sex-linked to the X or Y chromosomes; therefore, it does not exclusively affect daughters.
Skipping generations is a feature of autosomal recessive traits with carriers, not mitochondrial traits which are passed by every affected female.
Mitochondrial inheritance is not Y-linked; sons do not inherit it exclusively, although they will receive it from their mother.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": Eukaryotes have closed, circular, dsDNA molecules in their mitochondria... The human mitochondrial chromosome carries 22 tRNA genes. Mutations in these genes can cause human disease.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: A 12-year-old patient presents with progressive myoclonic epilepsy and proximal muscle weakness. A muscle biopsy reveals the presence of 'ragged red fibers.' The patient's mother has chronic fatigue and mild exercise intolerance, and his two sisters also show similar though milder neurologic symptoms. The father is completely healthy. Which inheritance pattern is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Autosomal recessive
Mitochondrial inheritance
Autosomal dominant
X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
correctOption: Mitochondrial inheritance
optionExplanations: Autosomal recessive would likely only affect a single generation of siblings and requires both parents to be carriers, which is inconsistent with an affected mother passing it to all children.
MERRF is a classic mitochondrial disorder; it is transmitted exclusively via the maternal line to all offspring, as only the oocyte provides mitochondria to the zygote.
Autosomal dominant would typically show transmission from the father if he were affected, and it would not explain the maternal-only transmission to all children in this case.
X-linked dominant would result in an affected father passing the trait to all daughters; here, the father is healthy, and maternal transmission to all offspring suggests mitochondrial DNA.
X-linked recessive would not affect the sisters (unless the father was also a carrier) and would not be transmitted by a mother to 100% of her female offspring.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": The human mitochondrial chromosome carries 22 tRNA genes... mutations in these genes are associated with myoclonic epilepsy (jerking muscle spasms) with ragged red fibers (MERRF)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: An infant is diagnosed with Phenylketonuria (PKU) during neonatal screening. The parents are phenotypically normal but are informed that for every subsequent pregnancy, there is a 25% risk of the child having the disease. What is the fundamental characteristic of this inheritance pattern?
options: Vertical transmission in every generation
Male-to-male transmission exclusively
Maternal transmission to all offspring
Horizontal transmission among siblings
Affects only hemizygous individuals
correctOption: Horizontal transmission among siblings
optionExplanations: Vertical transmission is characteristic of autosomal dominant traits, where every affected individual typically has an affected parent.
Male-to-male transmission is impossible in X-linked inheritance because a father passes his Y chromosome to his sons; PKU is autosomal and affects both sexes.
Maternal transmission to all offspring describes mitochondrial inheritance, not autosomal recessive traits like PKU.
Autosomal recessive disorders like PKU often manifest 'horizontally' within a single generation (among siblings) while parents and other ancestors appear unaffected (carriers).
Hemizygosity refers to genes on the X chromosome in males; PKU is caused by mutations in an autosomal gene (phenylalanine hydroxylase).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry": analysis of restriction fragment length polymorphism in a family with a child affected by phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal-recessive disease.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
statement: In the context of hypercholesterolemia, Type IIa hyperlipidemia is noted to be an autosomal dominant disorder. If one parent is heterozygous for the defective LDL receptor and the other parent is normal, what is the probability of their offspring inheriting the condition?
optionExplanations: 25% is the recurrence risk for autosomal recessive traits when both parents are carriers.
A 75% chance occurs only if both parents are heterozygous for an autosomal dominant trait.
A 100% chance would require at least one parent to be homozygous for the dominant mutation (AA).
A 0% chance would only occur if both parents were homozygous for the normal allele.
In autosomal dominant inheritance, a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a normal parent (aa) have a 1:1 ratio of offspring genotype (Aa or aa), resulting in a 50% probability of inheritance.
